changes.before: The Lord did so. A grievous swarm of flies came into the houses of Pharaoh and his servants and throughout all the land of Egypt. The land was ruined by these flies.
changes.after: The Lord did so. A very grievous swarm of flies came into the houses of Pharaoh and his servants and throughout all the land of Egypt. The land was ruined by these flies.
changes.reason: Musca gravissima is superlative (Douay “a very grievous swarm of flies”), and the column keeps such intensifiers elsewhere, as in 9:3 pestis valde gravis, “a very grievous plague”; “grievous” alone weakens it.

changes.before: He acted according to his word and removed the flies from Pharaoh, his servants, and his people. Not even one remained.
changes.after: The Lord acted according to Moses’ word and removed the flies from Pharaoh, his servants, and his people. Not even one remained.
changes.reason: Qui fecit juxta verbum illius means the Lord acted on Moses’ word; after 8:26 ends with Moses praying, “He acted according to his word” can be heard as Moses keeping his own promise, so both are named as the column already does in 8:9.

changes.before: “For the hand is of the Lord's throne, and the Lord's war against Amalek will be from generation to generation.”
changes.after: “For the hand of the Lord's throne, and the Lord's war, will be against Amalek from generation to generation.”
changes.reason: In Quia manus solii Domini, et bellum Domini erit contra Amalec both nouns are subjects of erit contra Amalec (as Douay); the supplied “is” created a separate, obscure clause (“the hand is of the Lord’s throne”) that the Latin lacks and that is hard to follow aloud.

changes.before: Moses said to the people, “Do not fear. God has come to test you, so that His fear may be in you and you may not sin.”
changes.after: Moses said to the people, “Do not fear. God has come to test you, so that the fear of Him may be in you and you may not sin.”
changes.reason: Ut terror illius esset in vobis means dread of God among the people, and “His fear” can be heard aloud as God’s own fear, so the object sense is made explicit.

changes.before: It is a sacrifice to the Lord, a perpetual offering throughout your generations, at the entrance of the tabernacle of the testimony before the Lord, where I will appoint to speak to you.
changes.after: It is a sacrifice to the Lord, a perpetual offering throughout your generations, at the entrance of the tabernacle of the testimony before the Lord, where I will arrange to speak to you.
changes.reason: Ubi constituam ut loquar ad te means where I will set things so as to speak with you; “appoint to speak” has no object and trips the ear, while “arrange to speak” keeps constituam.

changes.before: Leave Me, so that My wrath may blaze against them and I may destroy them; then I will make you into a great nation.”
changes.after: Let Me alone, so that My wrath may blaze against them and I may destroy them; then I will make you into a great nation.”
changes.reason: Dimitte me asks Moses not to hold God back (Douay “Let me alone”), but “Leave Me” is heard in modern English as “go away from Me.”

changes.before: If, then, I have found favor in Your sight, show me Your face, so that I may know You and find favor in Your eyes. Look upon this nation as Your people.”
changes.after: If, then, I have found favor in Your sight, show me Your face, so that I may know You and find favor in Your eyes. Look upon Your people, this nation.”
changes.reason: Respice populum tuum gentem hanc sets “this nation” in apposition to “Your people”; “as Your people” follows the Hebrew’s “consider that this nation is Your people” rather than the Vulgate.

changes.before: How will it be known that I and Your people have found favor in Your sight unless You walk with us, so that we may be glorified by all the peoples who dwell on the earth?”
changes.after: How can I and Your people know that we have found favor in Your sight unless You walk with us, so that we may be glorified by all the peoples who dwell on the earth?”
changes.reason: In quo enim scire poterimus ego et populus tuus invenisse nos gratiam has Moses and the people themselves knowing (“how shall we be able to know”), whereas the impersonal “How will it be known” follows the Hebrew.

changes.before: who keep mercy for thousands, who take away iniquity, crimes, and sins, and before whom no one is innocent of himself; who repay the iniquity of fathers upon children and grandchildren, to the third and fourth generation.”
changes.after: who keep mercy for thousands, who take away iniquity, crimes, and sins, and before whom no one is of himself innocent; who repay the iniquity of fathers upon children and grandchildren, to the third and fourth generation.”
changes.reason: Nullusque apud te per se innocens est means no one is innocent of himself (by his own merit) before God; “innocent of himself” is heard aloud as “not guilty of himself”, so the words are reordered without changing the sense.

changes.before: Take care never to enter friendships with the inhabitants of that land that may become your ruin.
changes.after: Take care never to enter friendships with the inhabitants of that land, friendships that may become your ruin.
changes.reason: The relative quæ sint tibi in ruinam refers to amicitias (the friendships), but read aloud “that land that may become your ruin” makes the land the ruin, so the antecedent is repeated.

changes.before: He made vessels for the table's various uses—dishes, bowls, cups, and censers in which drink offerings are to be offered—of pure gold.
changes.after: He made vessels of pure gold for the table's various uses—dishes, bowls, cups, and censers—in which drink offerings are to be offered.
changes.reason: In quibus offerenda sunt libamina follows ex auro puro and refers to the whole set of vessels (Douay “wherein the libations are to be offered”); placed straight after “censers” it is heard as if the censers held the drink offerings.

changes.before: He shall break open its wings, but shall not cut it apart or divide it with a blade. He shall burn it on the altar, with fire placed beneath the wood. It is a whole burnt offering and an offering of most pleasing fragrance to the Lord.
changes.after: He shall break its wings, but shall not cut it apart or divide it with a blade. He shall burn it on the altar, with fire placed beneath the wood. It is a whole burnt offering and an offering of most pleasing fragrance to the Lord.
changes.reason: Confringet ascellas ejus is “he shall break its wings” (Douay “the pinions”); “break open” reflects the Hebrew “tear it open by its wings” and suggests opening the bird’s body, which the Latin does not say.

changes.before: When the priest sees the leprous disease in the skin, the hairs changed to white, and the affected area lower than the rest of the skin and flesh, it is a lesion of leprous disease. The person shall be separated according to his judgment.
changes.after: When the priest sees the leprous disease in the skin, the hairs changed to white, and the affected area lower than the rest of the skin and flesh, it is a lesion of leprous disease. The person shall be separated according to the priest’s judgment.
changes.reason: Ad arbitrium ejus means the priest’s judgment (as 13:44 says outright); read aloud, “his judgment” sounds like the judgment of the person just named.

changes.before: The priest shall order everything to be taken out of the house before he enters it to see whether it is contaminated, so that everything in the house may not become unclean. Afterward he shall enter to examine the contamination in the house.
changes.after: The priest shall order everything to be taken out of the house before he enters it to see whether it is contaminated, so that nothing in the house may become unclean. Afterward he shall enter to examine the contamination in the house.
changes.reason: Ne immunda fiant omnia means none of the contents is to become unclean; “everything … may not become unclean” can be heard as “not all of it”.

changes.before: They shall immediately demolish it and throw its stones, wood, and all its plaster outside the town into an unclean place.
changes.after: They shall immediately demolish it and throw its stones, wood, and all its dust outside the town into an unclean place.
changes.reason: The Latin is universum pulverem (all the dust), as in pulvis erasus in 14:43 (“the dust scraped away”); “plaster” follows the Hebrew rather than the Vulgate.

changes.before: Do not turn to magicians or inquire of diviners, so that you become defiled through them. I am the Lord your God.
changes.after: Do not turn to magicians or inquire of diviners, and so become defiled through them. I am the Lord your God.
changes.reason: Ut polluamini per eos states the result of consulting them; after a prohibition, “so that you become defiled” sounds aloud like the purpose of not consulting them.

changes.before: You shall not offer the bread of your God from a foreigner's hand, or whatever else he wishes to give, for all these are damaged and blemished; you shall not accept them.
changes.after: You shall not offer bread to your God from a foreigner's hand, or whatever else he wishes to give, for all these are damaged and blemished; you shall not accept them.
changes.reason: The Latin has the dative panes Deo vestro (bread to your God), as the column renders panes Deo suo in 21:17 and 21:21; “the bread of your God” follows the Hebrew.

changes.before: For seven days you shall offer the Lord a sacrifice by fire. The seventh day shall be a day of special celebration and holiness; you shall do no servile work on it.
changes.after: For seven days you shall offer the Lord a sacrifice by fire. The seventh day shall be a day of greater celebration and holiness; you shall do no servile work on it.
changes.reason: The Vulgate uses comparatives, celebrior et sanctior (more solemn and more holy), deliberately ranking the seventh day above the days between; “special” loses the comparison.

changes.before: If your brother becomes poor and sells his small holding, and his relative wishes to do so, he may redeem what his brother sold.
changes.after: If your brother becomes poor and sells his small holding, and his relative is willing, he may redeem what his brother sold.
changes.reason: Latin et voluerit propinquus ejus (“and his kinsman is willing”) has no object; “wishes to do so” is heard aloud as wishing to sell, the only action named before it.

changes.before: you shall be subject to these curses: May the Lord make you a curse and an example to all among His people. May He cause your thigh to waste away and your swelling womb to burst.
changes.after: you shall be subject to these curses: May the Lord make you a curse and an example to all among His people. May He cause your thigh to rot and your swelling womb to burst.
changes.reason: Putrescere faciat femur tuum is “make your thigh rot” (Douay “rot”); “waste away” follows the Hebrew image, not the Vulgate’s putrefaction, which recurs in 5:22 and 5:27.

changes.before: May the cursed water enter your belly, and as your womb swells, may your thigh waste away. The woman shall answer: Amen, amen.
changes.after: May the cursed water enter your belly, and as your womb swells, may your thigh rot. The woman shall answer: Amen, amen.
changes.reason: Putrescat femur is “may the thigh rot”; keeps the Vulgate’s image consistent with 5:21 and 5:27 (computrescet).

changes.before: When she has drunk it, if she is defiled and, having despised her husband, is guilty of adultery, the water of the curse shall pass through her, her belly shall swell, and her thigh shall waste away. The woman shall become a curse and an example to all the people.
changes.after: When she has drunk it, if she is defiled and, having despised her husband, is guilty of adultery, the water of the curse shall pass through her, her belly shall swell, and her thigh shall rot. The woman shall become a curse and an example to all the people.
changes.reason: Computrescet femur is “the thigh shall rot (away)”; “waste away” loses the Vulgate’s image, matching the change in 5:21–22.

changes.before: When the people cried out to Moses, Moses prayed to the Lord, and the fire died away.
changes.after: When the people cried out to Moses, Moses prayed to the Lord, and the fire was swallowed up.
changes.reason: Absorptus est ignis means “the fire was swallowed up” (Douay); “died away” loses the Vulgate’s image of the fire being swallowed.

changes.before: Is it too little for you that you brought us out of a land flowing with milk and honey to kill us in the wilderness, unless you also lord it over us?
changes.after: Is it too little for you that you brought us out of a land flowing with milk and honey to kill us in the wilderness, that you must also lord it over us?
changes.reason: Nisi et dominatus fueris nostri means “without also lording it over us”; “unless” does not fit the question, so the sentence cannot be followed aloud.

changes.before: They shall take some of the ashes of the burning for sin and pour fresh water over them in a vessel.
changes.after: They shall take some of the ashes of the burning for sin and pour fresh running water over them in a vessel.
changes.reason: Aquas vivas is “living” (running) water, a ritual requirement; the column renders aquas vivas/viventes as “fresh running water” in Leviticus 14–15, while “fresh water” only means not salt.

changes.before: There is no idol in Jacob, nor is an image seen in Israel. The Lord his God is with him, and the shout of a king's victory is among him.
changes.after: There is no idol in Jacob, nor is an image seen in Israel. The Lord his God is with him, and the shout of a king's victory is in him.
changes.reason: Clangor victoriæ regis in illo is “in him” (Douay “in him”); “among him” with a singular pronoun trips the ear.

changes.before: God brought him out of Egypt, whose strength is like a rhinoceros.
changes.after: God brought him out of Egypt; his strength is like a rhinoceros.
changes.reason: Cujus fortitudo looks back to God (or Israel), never to Egypt, but read aloud “Egypt, whose strength” gives the rhinoceros strength to Egypt; “his” keeps the Latin’s own ambiguity.

changes.before: God brought him out of Egypt, whose strength is like a rhinoceros. They shall devour the nations that are his enemies, break their bones, and pierce them with arrows.
changes.after: God brought him out of Egypt; his strength is like a rhinoceros. They shall devour the nations that are his enemies, break their bones, and pierce them with arrows.
changes.reason: Same line as 23:22: cujus fortitudo refers to God (or Israel), not Egypt, and “Egypt, whose strength” misattaches it when heard.

changes.before: Of these, Nadab and Abihu died when they offered unauthorized fire before the Lord.
changes.after: Of these, Nadab and Abihu died when they offered strange fire before the Lord.
changes.reason: Ignem alienum is “strange fire”, as the 9 November pass already renders it in Numbers 3:4; “unauthorized” glosses the Hebrew zarah rather than giving the Vulgate’s image.

changes.before: clearing the land and dwelling in it. For I have given it to you as a possession,
changes.after: cleansing the land and dwelling in it. For I have given it to you as a possession,
changes.reason: Mundantes terram means cleansing or purifying the land (of its idols and their worshippers), matching emundabitur “shall be cleansed” in 35:34; “clearing” loses the purity image.

changes.before: The boundary shall curve from Azmon to the Wadi of Egypt and end at the shore of the Great Sea.
changes.after: The boundary shall curve from Azmon to the torrent of Egypt and end at the shore of the Great Sea.
changes.reason: Torrentem Ægypti is “the torrent of Egypt”, as the column renders it in Joshua 15:4 and 15:47 and as it renders torrens for the Zered, Arnon and Jabbok in this chunk; “Wadi” is not in the Latin.

changes.before: If anyone pushes a person out of hatred or throws something at him by an ambush,
changes.after: If anyone pushes a person out of hatred or throws something at him from ambush,
changes.reason: Per insidias means by lying in wait; “throws something at him by an ambush” trips the ear, while “from ambush” is the natural English for it.

changes.before: When the Lord your God has destroyed them before you, do not say in your heart: Because of my righteousness the Lord brought me in to possess this land. These nations have been destroyed because of their own wickedness.
changes.after: When the Lord your God has destroyed them before you, do not say in your heart: Because of my righteousness the Lord brought me in to possess this land, whereas these nations have been destroyed because of their own wickedness.
changes.reason: Cum propter impietates suas istæ deletæ sint nationes is Moses’ contrasting comment (“whereas these nations are destroyed for their wickedness”); as a separate sentence after the unquoted speech it is heard as part of what Israel must not say.

changes.before: I took the sinful thing you had made, the calf, burned it with fire, broke it into pieces, ground it entirely to dust, and threw it into the torrent flowing down the mountain.
changes.after: I took your sin that you had made, the calf, burned it with fire, broke it into pieces, ground it entirely to dust, and threw it into the torrent flowing down the mountain.
changes.reason: Peccatum vestrum quod feceratis, id est, vitulum deliberately calls the calf itself “your sin”; “the sinful thing” softens that image.

changes.before: After sitting on the throne of his kingdom, he shall write out for himself this repetition of the law in a scroll, receiving a model from the priests of the tribe of Levi.
changes.after: After sitting on the throne of his kingdom, he shall write out for himself this repetition of the law in a scroll, receiving a master copy from the priests of the tribe of Levi.
changes.reason: Accipiens exemplar a sacerdotibus means taking the text to copy from the priests; read aloud, “receiving a model” sounds like an object or pattern rather than a copy of the law.

changes.before: You shall be free of the innocent blood that was shed when you have done what the Lord commanded.
changes.after: When you have done what the Lord commanded, you shall be free of the innocent blood that was shed.
changes.reason: Cum feceris quod præcepit Dominus governs alienus eris; at the end of the sentence it is heard as dating the bloodshed (“shed when you have done what the Lord commanded”).

changes.before: But if the man finds the betrothed young woman in the countryside and seizes her and lies with her, he alone shall die.
changes.after: But if a man finds the betrothed young woman in the countryside and seizes her and lies with her, he alone shall die.
changes.reason: Vir here is any man (as in 22:23 aliquis); read aloud after 22:23, “the man” sounds like the betrothed husband.

changes.before: A man shall not take his father's wife or uncover his covering.
changes.after: A man shall not take his father's wife or uncover his father’s covering.
changes.reason: Operimentum ejus (non-reflexive) is the father’s covering; aloud, “his covering” sounds like the man’s own.

changes.before: the first husband may not receive her again as his wife, because she has been defiled and become abhorrent before the Lord. Do not cause the land the Lord your God gives you to possess to incur sin.
changes.after: the first husband may not receive her again as his wife, because she has been defiled and become abhorrent before the Lord. Do not bring sin upon the land the Lord your God gives you to possess.
changes.reason: Ne peccare facias terram tuam; the stacked “gives you to possess to incur sin” is hard to follow aloud.

changes.before: But if he refuses to take his brother's wife, who is due to him by law, the woman shall go to the city gate, appeal to the elders, and say: My husband's brother will not preserve his brother's name in Israel or take me as his wife.
changes.after: But if he refuses to take his brother's wife, who is due to him by law, the woman shall go to the city gate, appeal to the elders, and say: My husband's brother will not raise up his brother's name in Israel or take me as his wife.
changes.reason: Suscitare nomen repeats suscitabit semen of 25:5 (“raise up offspring”); “preserve” loses the deliberate echo and the image.

changes.before: Moses commanded us a law, the inheritance of the assembly of Jacob.
changes.after: Moses commanded us a law, the inheritance of the multitude of Jacob.
changes.reason: The Latin is hæreditatem multitudinis Jacob (the multitude of Jacob); “assembly” follows the Hebrew qehillat rather than the Vulgate.

changes.before: The others shouted together and urged one another on, pursuing them. When they had gone away from the city,
changes.after: But the men of Ai shouted together and urged one another on, pursuing them. When they had gone away from the city,
changes.reason: At illi refers to the men of Ai; “The others” read aloud can sound like “the rest of the multitude” with Joshua (8:5), so the pursuers are named.

changes.before: But do not stop yourselves. Pursue the enemies and strike down the hindmost of those fleeing. Do not let them enter the defenses of their cities, for the Lord God has handed them over to you.”
changes.after: But you, do not stand still. Pursue the enemies and strike down the hindmost of those fleeing. Do not let them enter the defenses of their cities, for the Lord God has handed them over to you.”
changes.reason: Vos autem nolite stare means “but you, do not stand still”; “do not stop yourselves” sounds like “do not hold yourselves back” when heard.

changes.before: Apart from the cities situated on hills and mounds, Israel burned the rest; Hazor alone, though very strongly fortified, he consumed with flames.
changes.after: Apart from the cities situated on hills and mounds, Israel burned the rest; Hazor alone, the most strongly fortified, he consumed with flames.
changes.reason: Unam tantum Asor munitissimam simply describes Hazor as the most strongly fortified city; the concessive “though” adds a contrast the Latin does not make.

changes.before: To the tribe of Levi he gave no possession. The sacrifices and sacrificial offerings of the Lord, the God of Israel, are its inheritance, as He told it.
changes.after: To the tribe of Levi he gave no possession. The sacrifices and sacrificial offerings of the Lord, the God of Israel, are its inheritance, as He told Levi.
changes.reason: Sicut locutus est illi means “as He said to it” (the tribe of Levi); “as He told it” sounds like “as He narrated it” when read aloud, so the tribe is named.

changes.before: Ehud came in to him. He was sitting alone in a cool upper room. Ehud said, “I have a message from God for you.” At once he rose from his throne.
changes.after: Ehud came in to him. He was sitting alone in a cool upper room. Ehud said, “I have a message from God for you.” At once the king rose from his throne.
changes.reason: Qui statim surrexit refers to Eglon, but right after “Ehud said” the bare “he rose” sounds aloud as if Ehud rose.

changes.before: So Jael, Heber's wife, took a tent peg and a hammer. She entered secretly and silently, placed the peg against his temple, and struck it with the hammer, driving it through his brain into the ground. His sleep joined with death; he failed and died.
changes.after: So Jael, Heber's wife, took a tent peg and a hammer. She entered secretly and silently, placed the peg against his temple, and struck it with the hammer, driving it through his brain into the ground. His sleep joined with death; his strength failed, and he died.
changes.reason: Defecit means he lost strength or swooned; “he failed” read aloud sounds like failure at a task.

changes.before: He collapsed between her feet; he failed and died. He rolled before her feet and lay lifeless and pitiful.
changes.after: He collapsed between her feet; his strength failed, and he died. He rolled before her feet and lay lifeless and pitiful.
changes.reason: Defecit, et mortuus est means he sank or swooned and died; “he failed” is unclear aloud (same wording as 4:21).

changes.before: When this was reported to Jotham, he went and stood on the summit of Mount Gerizim. Raising his voice, he cried out and said, “Hear me, men of Shechem, so that God may hear you.
changes.after: When this was reported to Jotham, he went and stood on the summit of Mount Gerizim. Raising his voice, he cried out and said, “Hear me, men of Shechem, and so may God hear you.
changes.reason: Ita audiat vos Deus is a wish formula (“so may God hear you”), not a purpose clause.

changes.before: God repaid the evil Abimelech had done against his father by killing his seventy brothers.
changes.after: God repaid the evil Abimelech had done against his father in killing his seventy brothers.
changes.reason: The ablative absolute describes Abimelech’s deed; “God repaid … by killing his seventy brothers” sounds aloud as if God did the killing.

changes.before: The angel of the Lord said to Manoah, “Let her abstain from all the things I told your wife.
changes.after: The angel of the Lord said to Manoah, “Let your wife abstain from all the things I told her.
changes.reason: Read aloud, “Let her … your wife” sounds like two different women; the Latin means the wife is to abstain from what was told to her.

changes.before: He struck them with a tremendous blow, so that in their stupefaction they drew calf against thigh. He went down and lived in the cave of the rock of Etam.
changes.after: He struck them with a tremendous blow, so that in their stupefaction they laid the calf of the leg upon the thigh. He went down and lived in the cave of the rock of Etam.
changes.reason: Suram femori imponerent means they laid the calf of the leg upon the thigh; the clipped “drew calf against thigh” is hard to follow aloud and sounds like an animal.

changes.before: The old man went out to them and said, “No, brothers, do not do this evil, for the man has entered my hospitality. Stop this folly.
changes.after: The old man went out to them and said, “No, brothers, do not do this evil, for the man has come into my house as a guest. Stop this folly.
changes.reason: Ingressus est homo hospitium meum means the man has come in under the old man’s hospitality as his guest; “entered my hospitality” trips the ear.

changes.before: He raises the needy from the dust and lifts the poor from the dung heap, to sit with princes and occupy a throne of glory. For the foundations of the earth belong to the Lord, and upon them He has set the world.
changes.after: He raises the needy from the dust and lifts the poor from the dung heap, to sit with princes and occupy a throne of glory. For the poles of the earth belong to the Lord, and upon them He has set the world.
changes.reason: The Vulgate has cardines terræ, the poles or hinges of the earth on which He set the world (Douay “the poles of the earth”), an image the column should keep rather than the Hebrew-style “foundations.”

changes.before: When you leave there, go farther on, and come to the oak of Tabor, three men going up to God at Bethel will meet you there. One will be carrying three young goats, another three loaves of bread, and another a flask of wine.
changes.after: When you leave there and go farther on and come to the oak of Tabor, three men going up to God at Bethel will meet you there. One will be carrying three young goats, another three loaves of bread, and another a flask of wine.
changes.reason: Cumque abieris inde, et ultra transieris, et veneris are all part of one temporal clause, but “leave there, go farther on, and come” sounds aloud like a string of commands that then collides with the main clause.

changes.before: he ran and stood over the Philistine, took his sword, and drew it from its sheath. He killed him and cut off his head. When the Philistines saw that their mightiest man was dead, they fled.
changes.after: David ran and stood over the Philistine, took his sword, and drew it from its sheath. He killed him and cut off his head. When the Philistines saw that their mightiest man was dead, they fled.
changes.reason: Cucurrit continues Vulgate 17:50, which has no row in this column, so the line follows 17:49 (“he fell facedown”) and a bare “he ran” sounds as if the fallen Philistine ran; naming David restores the subject.

changes.before: For all of you have conspired against me, and no one tells me, even when my own son makes a covenant with the son of Jesse. None of you feels sorrow for my plight or tells me that my son has stirred up my servant against me, to lie in wait for me as he does today.”
changes.after: For all of you have conspired against me, and no one tells me, especially since my own son has made a covenant with the son of Jesse. None of you feels sorrow for my plight or tells me that my son has stirred up my servant against me, to lie in wait for me as he does today.”
changes.reason: Maxime cum … inierit means “especially since … has made”: Saul is accusing them over a covenant already made, not a general or hypothetical case.

changes.before: he sent scouts and learned for certain that he had come there.
changes.after: he sent scouts and learned for certain that Saul had come there.
changes.reason: Latin quod illuc venisset has Saul as its implied subject; with David as the subject of “sent” and “learned”, “that he had come there” is heard aloud as David himself, so Saul is named.

changes.before: After him came Chileab, by Abigail, Nabal of Carmel's wife. The third was Absalom, son of Maacah, the daughter of Talmai king of Geshur.
changes.after: After him came Chileab, by Abigail, the wife of Nabal of Carmel. The third was Absalom, son of Maacah, the daughter of Talmai king of Geshur.
changes.reason: de Abigail uxore Nabal Carmeli; the stacked possessive “Nabal of Carmel’s wife” trips the ear, and the column elsewhere says “Abigail, the wife of Nabal of Carmel” (1 Sam 27:3, 30:5; 2 Sam 2:2).

changes.before: The king also said to his servants, “Do you not know that a great prince has fallen today in Israel?
changes.after: The king also said to his servants, “Do you not know that a prince and a very great man has fallen today in Israel?
changes.reason: Latin princeps et maximus gives two descriptors (a prince, and a very great one); “a great prince” merges them and drops the superlative.

changes.before: because You, Lord of hosts, God of Israel, have opened Your servant's ear, saying, ‘I will build you a house.’ Therefore Your servant has found the courage to pray this prayer to You.
changes.after: because You, Lord of hosts, God of Israel, have opened Your servant's ear, saying, ‘I will build you a house.’ Therefore Your servant has found it in his heart to pray this prayer to You.
changes.reason: invenit servus tuus cor suum keeps the image of the heart (Douay “found in his heart”); “found the courage” replaces the source’s image with an abstraction.

changes.before: The king said to Absalom, “No, my son, do not ask us all to come and burden you.” Though he pressed him, he would not go, but blessed him.
changes.after: The king said to Absalom, “No, my son, do not ask us all to come and burden you.” Though Absalom pressed him, he would not go, but blessed him.
changes.reason: Cum autem cogeret eum: Absalom presses the king; with two bare “he”s aloud it is unclear who pressed and who refused, so the presser is named.

changes.before: Joab entered the house before the king and said, “Today you have put to shame the faces of all your servants who saved your life and the lives of your sons, daughters, wives, and concubines.
changes.after: Joab went in to the king in the house and said, “Today you have put to shame the faces of all your servants who saved your life and the lives of your sons, daughters, wives, and concubines.
changes.reason: Ingressus Joab ad regem in domum means Joab went in to the king in the house; “entered the house before the king” sounds aloud as if Joab arrived ahead of David.

changes.before: He brought Saul's bones and the bones of his son Jonathan from there. They gathered the bones of those who had been fastened up,
changes.after: He brought Saul's bones and the bones of his son Jonathan from there. They gathered the bones of those who had been crucified,
changes.reason: Affixi fuerant refers back to the seven the Gibeonites crucified (crucifixerunt, 21:9), and the column says “crucify” there; “fastened up” is unclear when heard.

changes.before: When I got up in the morning to nurse my son, he appeared dead; but examining him more closely in the daylight, I discovered that he was not the son I had borne.”
changes.after: When I got up in the morning to nurse my son, I found him dead; but examining him more closely in the daylight, I discovered that he was not the son I had borne.”
changes.reason: Apparuit mortuus means the child was found to be dead, not that he only seemed dead; “appeared dead” misleads, since the child really had died (3:19).

changes.before: The basin's thickness was three unciae. Its rim was like the rim of a cup and the petal of an open lily. It held two thousand baths.
changes.after: The basin's thickness was three inches. Its rim was like the rim of a cup and the petal of an open lily. It held two thousand baths.
changes.reason: Trium unciarum is three inches (uncia = an inch, a twelfth of a foot); the untranslated Latin “unciae” means nothing to a listener.

changes.before: the two columns, the two rounded bands of the capitals upon the columns, and the two networks covering the two rounded bands on top of the columns;
changes.after: the two columns, the two cords of the capitals upon the columns, and the two networks covering the two cords on top of the columns;
changes.reason: Funiculos is “little cords” (the column renders the related linea/resticula as “cord” in 7:3 and 7:10); “rounded bands” imports the Hebrew gullot (bowls) rather than the Latin.

changes.before: the four hundred pomegranates for the two networks, two rows of pomegranates for each network, to cover the rounded bands of the capitals on top of the columns;
changes.after: the four hundred pomegranates for the two networks, two rows of pomegranates for each network, to cover the cords of the capitals on top of the columns;
changes.reason: Ad operiendos funiculos capitellorum: funiculi are cords, as in 7:27; “rounded bands” follows the Hebrew gullot, not the Vulgate.

changes.before: Nevertheless, you will not build Me a house. Your son, who will come from your own body, shall build a house for My name.’
changes.after: Nevertheless, you will not build Me a house. Your son, who will come forth from your loins, shall build a house for My name.’
changes.reason: Qui egredietur de renibus tuis keeps the image of coming forth from the loins (renes), which “from your own body” flattens; the image is easy to follow aloud.

changes.before: Hadad himself fled with Edomite men from his father's servants, to go to Egypt. Hadad was then a little boy.
changes.after: Hadad himself fled to go to Egypt, and with him Edomite men from among his father's servants. Hadad was then a little boy.
changes.reason: Fugit Adad ipse, et viri Idumæi de servis patris ejus cum eo: the Edomites were some of his father’s servants who fled with him, but “fled … from his father's servants” is heard aloud as fleeing from them.

changes.before: The messengers returned and reported to him. He sent back, saying, “May the gods do these things to me, and add to them, if Samaria's dust is enough for handfuls for all the people who follow me!”
changes.after: The messengers returned and reported to him. He sent back, saying, “May the gods do these things to me, and add to them, if the dust of Samaria is enough to give a handful to each of the people who follow me!”
changes.reason: Pugillis omnis populi means a handful for each of the people, and “enough for handfuls for all” trips the ear when read aloud.

changes.before: Elisha returned to Gilgal. There was a famine in the land, and the sons of the prophets were dwelling before him. He said to one of his servants, “Set out the large pot and cook a stew for the sons of the prophets.”
changes.after: Elisha returned to Gilgal. There was a famine in the land, and the sons of the prophets were dwelling before him. He said to one of his servants, “Put on the large pot and cook a stew for the sons of the prophets.”
changes.reason: Pone ollam grandem means to put the pot on the fire for cooking; “set out” sounds like laying it out on display.

changes.before: When he arrived, by then in the evening, he took the things from their hands, put them away in the house, and dismissed the men, who departed.
changes.after: When he arrived, it was already evening. He took the things from their hands, put them away in the house, and dismissed the men, who departed.
changes.reason: Cumque venisset jam vesperi is “when he had come, it now being evening”; the parenthetical “by then in the evening” is hard to follow aloud.

changes.before: let the priests receive according to their order, and let them repair the fabric of the house wherever they see repairs are needed.”
changes.after: let the priests receive it according to their order, and let them repair the fabric of the house wherever they see repairs are needed.”
changes.reason: Accipiant illam sacerdotes has the object illam (the money); without “it” the clause dangles when read aloud.

changes.before: No more than fifty horsemen, ten chariots, and ten thousand infantry were left to Jehoahaz from the people, for the king of Syria had killed them and reduced them to dust like the threshing on a threshing floor.
changes.after: No more than fifty horsemen, ten chariots, and ten thousand infantry were left to Jehoahaz from the people, for the king of Syria had killed them and made them like dust at the threshing on the threshing floor.
changes.reason: Redegerat quasi pulverem in tritura areae means he made them like dust at the threshing of the floor; “reduced them to dust like the threshing” garbles the comparison aloud.

changes.before: They worshiped filthy things, about which the Lord had commanded them not to do this thing.
changes.after: They worshiped filthy things, though the Lord had commanded them not to do this thing.
changes.reason: De quibus praecepit eis Dominus ne facerent verbum hoc is a Latin relative construction that becomes tangled in English as “about which … not to do this thing”; “though” keeps the sense and reads cleanly.

changes.before: That night the angel of the Lord came and struck down a hundred and eighty-five thousand in the Assyrian camp. When he rose at dawn, he saw all the bodies of the dead, and withdrew and departed.
changes.after: That night the angel of the Lord came and struck down a hundred and eighty-five thousand in the Assyrian camp. When the king rose at dawn, he saw all the bodies of the dead, and withdrew and departed.
changes.reason: The subject of diluculo surrexisset is the Assyrian king (named in 19:36), but right after “the angel of the Lord” the bare “he” sounds as if the angel rose and saw the dead.

changes.before: as this Passover celebrated for the Lord in Jerusalem in the eighteenth year of King Josiah.
changes.after: as this Passover was celebrated for the Lord in Jerusalem in the eighteenth year of King Josiah.
changes.reason: Sicut … factum est Phase istud is a finite clause (“as this Passover was kept”); without the verb the verse is a fragment that is hard to follow aloud after 23:22.

changes.before: For You, Lord my God, have revealed to Your servant that You will build him a house. Therefore Your servant has found confidence to pray before You.
changes.after: For You, Lord my God, have revealed to the ear of Your servant that You will build him a house. Therefore Your servant has found confidence to pray before You.
changes.reason: Revelasti auriculam servi tui keeps the image of uncovering the servant’s ear, which the current wording drops; it is easy to follow aloud.

changes.before: The sons of Amram: Aaron and Moses. Aaron was set apart, he and his sons forever, to minister in the Holy of Holies, to burn incense to the Lord according to His rite, and to bless His name forever.
changes.after: The sons of Amram: Aaron and Moses. Aaron was set apart, he and his sons forever, to minister in the Holy of Holies, to burn incense to the Lord according to his rite, and to bless His name forever.
changes.reason: Secundum ritum suum is reflexive and refers to Aaron (his priestly rite), in contrast with nomini ejus (God’s name); the capital “His” wrongly makes it God’s rite.

changes.before: For the altar on which incense was burned he gave purest gold, and for making from it the likeness of the chariot of the cherubim spreading their wings and covering the ark of the Lord's covenant.
changes.after: For the altar on which incense was burned he gave purest gold, from which was to be made the likeness of the chariot of the cherubim spreading their wings and covering the ark of the Lord's covenant.
changes.reason: Ut ex ipso fieret is a purpose clause about the same gold; “and for making from it” sounds like a separate allocation and is hard to follow aloud.

changes.before: because he was wiser and more powerful than all his sons, throughout all Judah and Benjamin and all the walled cities. He provided them abundant food and sought many wives.
changes.after: because he was wiser and more powerful than all Rehoboam’s sons, throughout all Judah and Benjamin and all the walled cities. He provided them abundant food and sought many wives.
changes.reason: Super omnes filios ejus means Rehoboam’s sons, but after a run of he/him/his referring to both Rehoboam and Abijah, “all his sons” sounds aloud like Abijah’s own sons.

changes.before: Amariah, your priest and high priest, will preside over matters concerning God. Zebadiah son of Ishmael, leader of the house of Judah, will oversee matters concerning the king's office. You have Levite officers before you. Be strong and act diligently, and the Lord will be with you in what is good.”
changes.after: Amariah, your priest and high priest, will preside over matters concerning God. Zebadiah son of Ishmael, leader of the house of Judah, will oversee matters concerning the king's office. You have the Levites as masters before you. Be strong and act diligently, and the Lord will be with you in what is good.”
changes.reason: The Vulgate reads habetisque magistros Levitas coram vobis (“you have the Levites as masters”), not the Hebrew’s “officers” (shoterim), and the column renders the Latin.

changes.before: She saw the king standing on the platform at the entrance, with the leaders and troops around him, and all the people of the land rejoicing, sounding trumpets, playing instruments of various kinds, and raising their voices in praise. She tore her clothes and cried, “Treason! Treason!”
changes.after: She saw the king standing on the step at the entrance, with the leaders and troops around him, and all the people of the land rejoicing, sounding trumpets, playing instruments of various kinds, and raising their voices in praise. She tore her clothes and cried, “Treason! Treason!”
changes.reason: The Latin has super gradum in introitu (“on the step at the entrance”); “platform” imports a different object not in the Vulgate.

changes.before: King Joash did not remember the mercy Jehoiada his father had shown him, but killed his son. As he died, he said, “May the Lord see and demand an account.”
changes.after: King Joash did not remember the mercy that Zechariah’s father Jehoiada had shown him, but killed his son. As he died, he said, “May the Lord see and demand an account.”
changes.reason: Jojada pater illius means Jehoiada, the father of Zechariah, whom Joash then killed; “Jehoiada his father” sounds as if Jehoiada were Joash’s father.

changes.before: Do not stiffen your necks as your fathers did. Give your hands in pledge to the Lord and come to His sanctuary, which He has consecrated forever. Serve the Lord God of your fathers, and His fierce anger will turn away from you.
changes.after: Do not stiffen your necks as your fathers did. Give your hands to the Lord and come to His sanctuary, which He has consecrated forever. Serve the Lord God of your fathers, and His fierce anger will turn away from you.
changes.reason: Tradite manus Domino is simply “give your hands to the Lord” (Douay “yield your hands”); “in pledge” adds an idea the Latin does not state.

changes.before: Hezekiah did all these things throughout Judah, doing what was good, right, and faithful before the Lord his God,
changes.after: Hezekiah did all these things throughout Judah, doing what was good, right, and true before the Lord his God,
changes.reason: The Latin triad is bonum et rectum, et verum; verum is “true”, and “faithful” follows the Hebrew emet rather than this column’s Latin.

changes.before: After this Sennacherib king of the Assyrians sent his servants to Jerusalem, while he and his whole army besieged Lachish, to Hezekiah king of Judah and all the people in the city, saying,
changes.after: After this Sennacherib king of the Assyrians sent his servants to Jerusalem—for he himself was besieging Lachish with his whole army—to Hezekiah king of Judah and all the people in the city, saying,
changes.reason: The Latin sets ipse enim … obsidebat Lachis in parentheses; read aloud, “while he and his whole army besieged Lachish, to Hezekiah” leaves “to Hezekiah” dangling, so the aside is marked off with dashes.

changes.before: Therefore He brought upon them the commanders of the king of the Assyrians' army. They captured Manasseh and brought him to Babylon bound in chains and fetters.
changes.after: Therefore He brought upon them the commanders of the army of the king of the Assyrians. They captured Manasseh and brought him to Babylon bound in chains and fetters.
changes.reason: Principes exercitus regis Assyriorum; the stacked possessive “the king of the Assyrians’ army” trips the ear, so the phrase follows the Latin order.

changes.before: He told the Levites, through whose instruction all Israel was consecrated to the Lord, “Place the ark in the sanctuary of the temple Solomon son of David, king of Israel, built, for you will no longer carry it. Now minister to the Lord your God and His people Israel.
changes.after: He told the Levites, through whose instruction all Israel was consecrated to the Lord, “Place the ark in the sanctuary of the temple built by Solomon son of David, king of Israel, for you will no longer carry it. Now minister to the Lord your God and His people Israel.
changes.reason: Quod ædificavit Salomon filius David rex Israël; with the verb held to the end of a long name and title, “king of Israel, built” is hard to follow aloud.

changes.before: He brought upon them the king of the Chaldeans, who killed their young men with the sword in their sanctuary. He spared neither young man nor virgin, neither the old nor even the decrepit; He delivered them all into his hands.
changes.after: He brought upon them the king of the Chaldeans, who killed their young men with the sword in the house of His sanctuary. He spared neither young man nor virgin, neither the old nor even the decrepit; He delivered them all into his hands.
changes.reason: The Vulgate has in domo sanctuarii sui (Douay “in the house of his sanctuary”), God’s own sanctuary; “their sanctuary” follows the Hebrew miqdasham, not the Latin.

changes.before: “Thus says Cyrus king of the Persians: The Lord God of heaven has given me all the kingdoms of the earth and commanded me to build Him a house in Jerusalem in Judah. Whoever among you belongs to all His people, may the Lord his God be with him, and let him go up.”
changes.after: “Thus says Cyrus king of the Persians: The Lord God of heaven has given me all the kingdoms of the earth and commanded me to build Him a house in Jerusalem in Judah. Who is there among you of all His people? May the Lord his God be with him, and let him go up.”
changes.reason: Quis ex vobis est in omni populo ejus? is a question (Douay “Who is there among you of all his people?”); “Whoever among you belongs to all His people” is confusing aloud.

changes.before: All the silver and gold you find throughout the province of Babylon that the people wish to offer, and whatever the priests freely offer to the house of their God in Jerusalem,
changes.after: All the silver and gold you find throughout the province of Babylon, and what the people wish to offer, and whatever the priests freely offer to the house of their God in Jerusalem,
changes.reason: The Latin lists two separate sources (quodcumque inveneris … et populus offerre voluerit, “whatever you find … and what the people wish to offer”), but the English turned the second into a clause restricting the first.

changes.before: The king said to me, with the queen sitting beside him, “How long will your journey last, and when will you return?” It pleased the king, and he sent me; I set a time for him.
changes.after: The king, and the queen who sat beside him, said to me, “How long will your journey last, and when will you return?” It pleased the king, and he sent me; I set a time for him.
changes.reason: In Dixitque mihi rex, et regina quæ sedebat juxta eum the queen is a second subject of dixit (Douay: “the king said to me, and the queen that sat by him”), so the Vulgate has her speak too, not merely sit by.

changes.before: You made known to them Your holy Sabbath and commanded them commandments, observances, and law through Your servant Moses.
changes.after: You made known to them Your holy Sabbath and laid down for them commandments, observances, and law through Your servant Moses.
changes.reason: “Commanded them commandments” trips the ear; “laid down for them” keeps the force of præcepisti without the jingle.

changes.before: He made a large storeroom for himself, where previously they had stored the offerings, incense, vessels, and the tithe of grain, wine, and oil, the portions for the Levites, singers, and gatekeepers, and the first offerings for the priests.
changes.after: He made a large storeroom for him, where previously they had stored the offerings, incense, vessels, and the tithe of grain, wine, and oil, the portions for the Levites, singers, and gatekeepers, and the first offerings for the priests.
changes.reason: In this Vulgate sibi points to Tobiah, as 13:7 makes explicit (ut faceret ei thesaurum, “by making him a storeroom”), so “for himself” wrongly makes Eliashib the beneficiary.

changes.before: as is how Mordecai, of Jewish descent, became second to King Ahasuerus, great among the Jews and beloved by the multitude of his brothers, seeking the good of his people and speaking for the peace of his descendants.
changes.after: and how Mordecai, of Jewish descent, was second to King Ahasuerus, great among the Jews and beloved by the multitude of his brothers, seeking the good of his people and speaking for the peace of his descendants.
changes.reason: Et quomodo … fuerit continues what “is recorded” in 10:2 (“and how Mordecai … was second”); “as is how … became” is hard to follow aloud and fuerit means “was”, not “became”.

changes.before: He seems well-watered before the sun comes, and at his rising his shoot comes forth.
changes.after: He seems well-watered before the sun comes, and at its rising his shoot comes forth.
changes.reason: In ortu suo is the rising of the sun just named (Douay’s old “his” for the sun); read aloud in modern English, “at his rising” sounds like the man’s rising.

changes.before: a land of misery and darkness, where the shadow of death and no order, but everlasting horror, dwell.
changes.after: a land of misery and darkness, where there is the shadow of death and no order, but everlasting horror dwells.
changes.reason: The row ran “shadow of death and no order” as a joint subject of “dwell”, which is hard to follow aloud; the Latin has “where [there is] the shadow of death and no order, but everlasting horror dwells.”

changes.before: Does not the ear judge words, and the eater's palate their flavor?
changes.after: Does not the ear judge words, and the eater’s palate the taste?
changes.reason: “Their flavor” made the taste belong to the words; the Latin “saporem” is simply the palate’s judging of taste.

changes.before: Their cow conceives and does not miscarry; their cow gives birth and is not deprived of her young.
changes.after: Their cattle conceive and do not miscarry; their cow gives birth and is not deprived of her young.
changes.reason: The Latin uses two words (bos, vacca); repeating “their cow” twice sounds like a slip when read aloud.

changes.before: He has set a limit to darkness and examines the end of all things, even the stone of gloom and the shadow of death.
changes.after: He has set a time for darkness and examines the end of all things, even the stone of gloom and the shadow of death.
changes.reason: The Vulgate reads “tempus posuit tenebris” (a time), not the Hebrew-derived “limit”.

changes.before: He said to humanity: Behold, the fear of the Lord is wisdom, and to turn away from evil is understanding.
changes.after: He said to humanity: Behold, the fear of the Lord, that is wisdom, and to turn away from evil is understanding.
changes.reason: Keeps the Vulgate’s emphatic “ipsa est sapientia” (that is wisdom), which the row had flattened.

changes.before: If I wished to go to them, I sat first. Though I sat like a king with an army surrounding him, I was nevertheless a comforter of mourners.
changes.after: If I wished to go to them, I sat in the first place. Though I sat like a king with an army surrounding him, I was nevertheless a comforter of mourners.
changes.reason: Sedebam primus means Job took the chief seat among them; “I sat first” sounds aloud as if he merely sat down before anyone else.

changes.before: His soul has drawn near to corruption, and his life to deadly agents.
changes.after: His soul has drawn near to corruption, and his life to the things that bring death.
changes.reason: Mortiferis means the death-bringing things (Douay “the destroyers”); “deadly agents” sounds like spies or poisons when read aloud.

changes.before: Therefore the ungodly will not rise in judgment, nor sinners in the assembly of the just,
changes.after: Therefore the ungodly will not rise again in judgment, nor sinners in the assembly of the just,
changes.reason: The Vulgate has non resurgent (“will not rise again”), the reading on which the Latin tradition built its resurrection sense of this verse; plain “rise” drops the re-.

changes.before: for You will bless the just. Lord, You have surrounded us with Your goodwill as with a shield.
changes.after: for You will bless the just. Lord, You have crowned us with Your goodwill as with a shield.
changes.reason: The Latin has coronasti (“You have crowned”), the Vulgate’s own image; “surrounded” follows the Hebrew rather than the Clementine text.

changes.before: See, he has labored with injustice; he has conceived trouble and given birth to iniquity.
changes.after: See, he has been in labor with injustice; he has conceived trouble and given birth to iniquity.
changes.reason: Parturiit is the pains of childbirth, opening the series parturiit–concepit–peperit; “labored with” sounds aloud like “worked alongside” and loses the birth image.

changes.before: Rescue my soul from the spear, God, and my only life from the dog's power.
changes.after: Rescue my soul from the spear, God, and my only life from the hand of the dog.
changes.reason: Restores the Latin image “de manu canis” (from the hand of the dog), which the row had flattened to “the dog’s power”.

changes.before: But the Lord will not abandon him in his hands or condemn him when judgment is given against him.
changes.after: But the Lord will not abandon him in his hands or condemn him when he is judged.
changes.reason: “Cum judicabitur illi” means when he is judged; “when judgment is given against him” implied the verdict was already adverse, contradicting “nor condemn him”.

changes.before: Even the man at peace with me, in whom I trusted, who ate my bread, has greatly sought to trip me up.
changes.after: Even the man at peace with me, in whom I trusted, who ate my bread, has greatly tripped me up.
changes.reason: Magnificavit super me supplantationem says the trusted friend actually tripped me up in a big way (Douay “hath greatly supplanted me”); “sought to” turns a done betrayal into a mere attempt.

changes.before: I will enter to the altar of God, to God who gladdens my youth. I will praise You with the lyre, God, my God.
changes.after: I will go in to the altar of God, to God who gladdens my youth. I will praise You with the lyre, God, my God.
changes.reason: “Enter to the altar” trips the ear; “go in to the altar of God” renders introibo ad altare Dei plainly and keeps the familiar wording of this liturgical verse.

changes.before: All her glory, the king's daughter's, is within, in golden fringes,
changes.after: All the glory of the king’s daughter is within, in golden fringes,
changes.reason: The Latin ejus … filiae regis is a resumptive genitive; the doubled possessive “her glory, the king’s daughter’s” is hard to follow aloud, and the plain form says the same.

changes.before: Seeing it, they were amazed in this way, troubled and shaken.
changes.after: They saw it and so were amazed; they were troubled, they were shaken.
changes.reason: Sic here means “thereupon/accordingly,” not “in this way,” and the three verbs admirati sunt, conturbati sunt, commoti sunt are a deliberate cumulative series that reads more clearly aloud when kept as such.

changes.before: He will enter among the generations of his fathers and will not see light forever.
changes.after: He will enter among the generations of his fathers and will never see light.
changes.reason: Usque in aeternum non videbit lumen means he will never see light; “will not see light forever” can be heard as “will not see light permanently.”

changes.before: The Lord said, “I will turn back from Bashan; I will turn back into the depth of the sea,
changes.after: The Lord said, “I will turn them from Bashan; I will turn them into the depth of the sea,
changes.reason: Convertam is transitive here (Douay “I will turn them from Basan … into the depth of the sea”); “I will turn back from Bashan” makes it sound as if the Lord Himself retreats.

changes.before: Make vows and fulfill them to the Lord your God, all around Him who bring gifts to the fearsome One,
changes.after: Make vows and fulfill them to the Lord your God, all you around Him who bring gifts to the fearsome One,
changes.reason: Omnes qui in circuitu ejus affertis munera is second person (“all you who bring”), and without “you” the line sounds ungrammatical when read aloud.

changes.before: perhaps I would have humbled their enemies for nothing and sent My hand against those who troubled them.
changes.after: perhaps I would have humbled their enemies with ease and sent My hand against those who troubled them.
changes.reason: Pro nihilo here means “as nothing,” i.e. with no effort (Douay “soon”); English “for nothing” is heard as “in vain” or “without reason.”

changes.before: The dwelling in you is as of all who rejoice.
changes.after: The dwelling in you is like that of all who rejoice.
changes.reason: Sicut lætantium omnium habitatio means the dwelling in Zion is like the dwelling of all who rejoice; “as of all who rejoice” is hard to follow aloud.

changes.before: the arrow flying by day, the affair passing through the darkness, the assault, or the noonday demon.
changes.after: the arrow flying by day, the trouble that walks about in the darkness, the assault, or the noonday demon.
changes.reason: Negotium perambulans is the trouble or plague walking about in the dark; to a modern listener “the affair” suggests a romance, and perambulante is better heard as “walks about.”

changes.before: Whoever acts proudly will not dwell within my house; whoever speaks unjust things did not conduct himself rightly before my eyes.
changes.after: Whoever acts proudly will not dwell within my house; whoever speaks unjust things did not prosper before my eyes.
changes.reason: Non direxit is intransitive here (“was not set straight, did not prosper,” Douay “did not prosper”), describing the liar’s fate before the king, not his conduct.

changes.before: Let His mercies and His wonders for the children of men give thanks to the Lord.
changes.after: Let His mercies give thanks to the Lord, and His wonders to the children of men.
changes.reason: Confiteantur Domino misericordiae ejus, et mirabilia ejus filiis hominum pairs “His mercies … to the Lord” with “His wonders … to the children of men”; read aloud, the current wording loses that parallel and makes “for the children of men” sound like a description of the wonders.

changes.before: Let His mercies and His wonders for the children of men give thanks to the Lord.
changes.after: Let His mercies give thanks to the Lord, and His wonders to the children of men.
changes.reason: Confiteantur Domino misericordiae ejus, et mirabilia ejus filiis hominum pairs “His mercies … to the Lord” with “His wonders … to the children of men”; read aloud, the current wording loses that parallel and makes “for the children of men” sound like a description of the wonders.

changes.before: Let His mercies and His wonders for the children of men give thanks to the Lord.
changes.after: Let His mercies give thanks to the Lord, and His wonders to the children of men.
changes.reason: Confiteantur Domino misericordiae ejus, et mirabilia ejus filiis hominum pairs “His mercies … to the Lord” with “His wonders … to the children of men”; read aloud, the current wording loses that parallel and makes “for the children of men” sound like a description of the wonders.

changes.before: Let His mercies and His wonders for the children of men give thanks to the Lord.
changes.after: Let His mercies give thanks to the Lord, and His wonders to the children of men.
changes.reason: Confiteantur Domino misericordiae ejus, et mirabilia ejus filiis hominum pairs “His mercies … to the Lord” with “His wonders … to the children of men”; read aloud, the current wording loses that parallel and makes “for the children of men” sound like a description of the wonders.

changes.before: Will You not, God, who have rejected us? And will You not go out, God, with our armies?
changes.after: Will it not be You, God, who have rejected us? And will You not go out, God, with our armies?
changes.reason: Nonne tu, Deus answers the previous “Who will lead me…?”; “Will You not, God” sounds like an unfinished question when read aloud.

changes.before: Your wife is like a fruitful vine within your house; your children are like young olive trees around your table.
changes.after: Your wife is like a fruitful vine on the sides of your house; your children are like young olive trees around your table.
changes.reason: In lateribus domus tuae is “on the sides of your house”, the vine’s image of clinging to the walls, which “within your house” loses.

changes.before: If You kill sinners, God, then, men of blood, turn away from me,
changes.after: If You kill sinners, God, then turn away from me, you men of blood,
changes.reason: Viri sanguinum is a vocative addressed to the men of blood; “then, men of blood, turn away” trips aloud and can sound like a list, so the address is moved to the end and marked with “you”.

changes.before: Do not hand me over to the sinner because of my desire, Lord. They have plotted against me; do not abandon me, lest they be exalted.
changes.after: Do not hand me over to the sinner against my desire, Lord. They have plotted against me; do not abandon me, lest they be exalted.
changes.reason: A desiderio meo means away from or against my desire (Douay “from my desire”), not “because of my desire”, which makes the psalmist’s own wish the cause.

changes.before: Can a man hide fire in his embrace without his clothes burning,
changes.after: Can a man hide fire in his bosom without his clothes burning,
changes.reason: In sinu suo is the fold of the garment at the chest, where hidden fire would set the clothes alight; “embrace” blurs the source’s image.

changes.before: Whoever repays evil for good will have evil never leave his house.
changes.after: Whoever repays evil for good, evil will not leave his house.
changes.reason: Qui reddit mala pro bonis, non recedet malum de domo ejus keeps “evil” as the subject of the second clause; “will have evil never leave his house” trips the ear, and the Latin’s own broken construction reads cleanly aloud.

changes.before: There are many thoughts in a man's heart, but the Lord's will will remain.
changes.after: There are many thoughts in a man’s heart, but the will of the Lord will endure.
changes.reason: Voluntas autem Domini permanebit; “the Lord’s will will remain” stumbles on the doubled “will” when read aloud.

changes.before: A ruler who gladly hears lying words has all his servants wicked.
changes.after: A ruler who gladly hears lying words has only wicked servants.
changes.reason: Omnes ministros habet impios means all his ministers are wicked; “has all his servants wicked” is hard to follow aloud.

changes.before: Do not, Lemuel, do not give wine to kings, for there is no secret where drunkenness reigns,
changes.after: Do not give to kings, Lemuel, do not give wine to kings, for there is no secret where drunkenness reigns,
changes.reason: Noli regibus, o Lamuel, noli regibus dare vinum deliberately repeats both “do not” and “to kings”; the current wording keeps only the first repetition.

changes.before: I learned that all the works God has done endure forever. We cannot add anything to them or take anything away from the things God has done so that He may be feared.
changes.after: I learned that all the works God has done endure forever. We cannot add anything to them or take anything away from them; God has made them so that He may be feared.
changes.reason: Quae fecit Deus ut timeatur says God made these things so that He may be feared; read aloud, “take anything away from the things God has done so that He may be feared” sounds as if our taking away is what makes Him feared.

changes.before: I judged happier than either the one who has not yet been born and has not seen the evils done under the sun.
changes.after: I judged the one who has not yet been born, and has not seen the evils done under the sun, happier than either.
changes.reason: Feliciorem utroque judicavi qui necdum natus est means the unborn one is judged happier than both the dead and the living; the current word order makes the unborn the thing compared against, reversing the sense when heard.

changes.before: Wisdom with riches is more useful and benefits those who see the sun more.
changes.after: Wisdom with riches is more useful and is of greater benefit to those who see the sun.
changes.reason: Magis prodest videntibus solem means wisdom benefits the living more; the trailing “more” makes it sound as if those who see the sun more are meant.

changes.before: If the spirit of one who has power rises against you, do not abandon your place, because care will bring the greatest sins to an end.
changes.after: If the spirit of one who has power rises against you, do not abandon your place, because healing will bring the greatest sins to an end.
changes.reason: Curatio is healing or cure (Douay “cure”), the source’s remedy image, whereas “care” is heard as caution.

changes.before: Before the silver cord breaks and the golden band draws back, the pitcher is shattered at the spring, and the wheel is broken at the cistern,
changes.after: Before the silver cord breaks and the golden band draws back, and the pitcher is shattered at the spring and the wheel is broken at the cistern,
changes.reason: All four clauses depend on the single antequam joined by et; with no “and” before it, “the pitcher is shattered” is heard as a main statement rather than part of the “before” series.

changes.before: For God will exempt no one's person or stand in awe of anyone's greatness, because He Himself made small and great and cares equally for all.
changes.after: For God will exempt no one or stand in awe of anyone's greatness, because He Himself made small and great and cares equally for all.
changes.reason: Non subtrahet personam cujusquam is an idiom for exempting no one; “exempt no one's person” trips the ear without adding meaning.

changes.before: When the nations united in agreement to do evil, she recognized the righteous man, kept him blameless before God, and preserved him strong in compassion for his son.
changes.after: When the nations united in agreement to do evil, she recognized the righteous man, kept him blameless before God, and preserved him strong in the face of his compassion for his son.
changes.reason: In filii misericordia fortem custodivit means she kept Abraham strong against his pity for his son (the binding of Isaac); “strong in compassion” turns the point around.

changes.before: While these were being brought low through the exposure of the murdered infants, You unexpectedly gave the others abundant water,
changes.after: While these were being brought low as a rebuke for the murdered infants, You unexpectedly gave the others abundant water,
changes.reason: In traductione infantium occisorum means in public reproof for the infants they had killed; “exposure” suggests the exposing of infants, which the Latin does not say here.

changes.before: But empty are all people in whom there is no knowledge of God. From the good things that are seen they could not understand Him who is, nor, attending to the works, did they recognize who the craftsmaker was.
changes.after: But empty are all people in whom there is no knowledge of God. From the good things that are seen they could not understand Him who is, nor, attending to the works, did they recognize who the craftsman was.
changes.reason: Artifex is “craftsman,” the word the column uses at 14:2; “craftsmaker” is not an English word and trips the ear.

changes.before: In place of those torments, You provided well for Your people: You gave them a new taste to satisfy their delightful desire, preparing quail as food for them.
changes.after: In place of those torments, You provided well for Your people: You gave them a new taste to satisfy their desire for delight, preparing quail as food for them.
changes.reason: Concupiscentiam delectamenti sui is their craving for what delights them; “delightful desire” wrongly makes the desire itself delightful.

changes.before: A human being does kill through malice; but when the spirit has departed, it will not return, nor will he call back the soul that has been received away.
changes.after: A human being does kill through malice; but when the spirit has departed, it will not return, nor will he call back the soul that has been taken.
changes.reason: Animam quae recepta est is the soul that has been taken up; “received away” is not natural English and obscures the sense aloud.

changes.before: When they planned to kill the infants of the righteous, and one exposed child had been delivered, You took away a multitude of their children to expose them, and destroyed them together in mighty water.
changes.after: When they planned to kill the infants of the righteous, and one exposed child had been delivered, You took away a multitude of their children as a rebuke to them, and destroyed them together in mighty water.
changes.reason: In traductionem illorum means to shame or rebuke the Egyptians; “to expose them” sounds as if the children themselves were exposed.

changes.before: The greater you are, humble yourself in all things, and you will find favor before God,
changes.after: The greater you are, the more humble yourself in all things, and you will find favor before God,
changes.reason: Quanto magnus es, humilia te is a correlative (“the greater … the more”); without “the more” the sentence does not hold together when read aloud.

changes.before: Son, take care over the time, and avoid evil.
changes.after: Son, observe the time, and avoid evil.
changes.reason: Conserva tempus means watch or observe the right time; “take care over the time” is unclear aloud.

changes.before: Do not take pleasure in the wrongdoing of the unjust, knowing that the ungodly will not be pleasing all the way to the realm of the dead.
changes.after: Do not take pleasure in the wrongdoing of the unjust, knowing that the ungodly will not find favor even down to the realm of the dead.
changes.reason: Usque ad inferos non placebit impius says the ungodly will not please (find favor) even down to the grave; “will not be pleasing all the way to” is hard to follow aloud.

changes.before: Son, do not let your activities extend to many things; even if you become rich, you will not be free from wrongdoing. For if you pursue, you will not catch up; and if you run ahead, you will not escape.
changes.after: Son, do not let your activities extend to many things; and if you become rich, you will not be free from wrongdoing. For if you pursue, you will not catch up; and if you run ahead, you will not escape.
changes.reason: Et si dives fueris is “and if you become rich” (by busying yourself with many things), not a concession; “even if” suggests riches might have been expected to free one from fault.

changes.before: There is a man who labors and hurries and suffers, yet is ungodly; all the more, he will not prosper.
changes.after: There is a man who labors and hurries and suffers, yet is ungodly, and so much the less will he prosper.
changes.reason: Et tanto magis non abundabit means “and so much the more will he fall short”; “all the more, he will not prosper” is confusing aloud.

changes.before: The account of sinners is hateful, and their laughter is in the pleasures of sin.
changes.after: The talk of sinners is hateful, and their laughter is in the pleasures of sin.
changes.reason: Narratio peccantium is the sinners’ talk or discourse; “account” can be heard as their reckoning or record.

changes.before: Nevertheless, be more steadfast toward one of lowly spirit, and do not drag him along over almsgiving.
changes.after: Nevertheless, be more steadfast toward one of lowly spirit, and do not keep him waiting for alms.
changes.reason: Pro eleemosyna non trahas illum means do not put him off or delay him over alms (trahere = draw out); “drag him along” suggests physical treatment.

changes.before: A sinful man will avoid correction and find a comparison to suit his own will.
changes.after: A sinful man will avoid correction and find an excuse to suit his own will.
changes.reason: Inveniet comparationem here means he finds a precedent or pretext that suits him (Douay “excuse”); “a comparison” makes no sense aloud.

changes.before: But because of accusation, bear bitter mourning for him for one day, and take comfort because of the sorrow.
changes.after: But to avoid being spoken against, bear bitter mourning for him for one day, and take comfort because of the sorrow.
changes.reason: Propter delaturam means for fear of being reported or ill spoken of if one does not mourn; “because of accusation” leaves the listener unsure whose accusation.

changes.before: Many will praise his wisdom, and it will not be erased forever.
changes.after: Many will praise his wisdom, and it will never be erased.
changes.reason: Usque in sæculum non delebitur is “it will never be blotted out”; “will not be erased forever” can be heard as only a temporary erasure.

changes.before: A man who looks toward another's table does not have a life to be reckoned as a livelihood, for he feeds his soul with another's food.
changes.after: A man who looks toward another's table—his life is not to be reckoned a living, for he feeds his soul with another's food.
changes.reason: Non est vita ejus in cogitatione victus says his life does not count as a living; “does not have a life to be reckoned as a livelihood” is hard to follow aloud.

changes.before: commanding the people before them, and by the power of prudence speaking most holy words to peoples;
changes.after: commanding the people of their own day, and by the power of prudence speaking most holy words to peoples;
changes.reason: In praesenti populo means the people of their own time; read aloud, “the people before them” sounds like their predecessors or a crowd in front of them.

changes.before: nor like Joseph, who was born a man who became a leader of brothers, the nation's support, ruler of brothers, the people's firm foundation.
changes.after: nor like Joseph, who was born a man, a leader of brothers, the nation's support, ruler of brothers, the people's firm foundation.
changes.reason: Natus est homo princeps fratrum says Joseph was born a leader of his brothers; “who became” adds a later change that the Latin does not state.

changes.before: and delivered my body from destruction, from the snare of an unjust tongue and the lips of those who work falsehood. And in the sight of those standing by You became my Helper.
changes.after: and delivered my body from destruction, from the snare of an unjust tongue and the lips of those who work falsehood. And You became my Helper in the sight of those standing by.
changes.reason: Read aloud, “those standing by You” sounds like people standing beside God, whereas in conspectu astantium means in the sight of the bystanders.

changes.before: The Lord will create over every place on Mount Zion, and wherever He has been invoked, a cloud by day, and smoke and the brightness of flaming fire by night; for over all the glory there will be protection.
changes.after: The Lord will create over every place on Mount Zion, and wherever He has been invoked, a cloud and smoke by day, and the brightness of flaming fire by night; for over all the glory there will be protection.
changes.reason: The Latin pairs nubem per diem et fumum (cloud and smoke by day) against splendorem ignis flammantis in nocte; the English moved the smoke to the night.

changes.before: Say to him: See that you remain quiet. Do not be afraid, and do not let your heart dread these two stumps of smoking firebrands, the furious anger of Rezin king of Syria and of the son of Remaliah.
changes.after: Say to him: See that you remain quiet. Do not be afraid, and do not let your heart dread these two tails of smoking firebrands, the furious anger of Rezin king of Syria and of the son of Remaliah.
changes.reason: The Vulgate has duabus caudis titionum fumigantium, “two tails of smoking firebrands,” and the source’s image of tails should be kept.

changes.before: but he will judge the poor with righteousness and reprove fairly for the meek of the earth. He will strike the earth with the rod of his mouth and kill the wicked with the breath of his lips.
changes.after: but he will judge the poor with righteousness and reprove with equity on behalf of the meek of the earth. He will strike the earth with the rod of his mouth and kill the wicked with the breath of his lips.
changes.reason: Arguet in aequitate pro mansuetis terrae means he will reprove with equity on behalf of the meek; “reprove fairly for” is hard to follow aloud.

changes.before: How have you fallen from heaven, morning star, who used to rise at dawn? Have you collapsed upon the earth, you who wounded the nations?
changes.after: How have you fallen from heaven, morning star, who used to rise at dawn? How you have collapsed upon the earth, you who wounded the nations?
