changes.reason: The second clause still hangs on quomodo (“how … corruisti in terram”), a lament parallel to “How have you fallen,” not a yes-or-no question as “Have you collapsed” makes it.

changes.before: Judah's covering will be exposed, and on that day you will look to the armory of the House of the Forest.
changes.after: Judah's covering will be exposed, and on that day you will see the armory of the House of the Forest.
changes.reason: The Vulgate has simply videbis armamentarium (“you will see the armory”); “look to” adds a sense of relying on it that the Latin does not carry.

changes.before: He will wind you round and round with affliction; He will throw you like a ball into a broad and spacious land. There you will die, and there will be your glorious chariot, you disgrace to your master's house.
changes.after: He will crown you with a crown of affliction; He will throw you like a ball into a broad and spacious land. There you will die, and there will be your glorious chariot, you disgrace to your master's house.
changes.reason: Coronas coronabit te tribulatione is the Vulgate’s image of a crown of tribulation (as in the Douay); “wind you round and round” renders the Hebrew, not the Latin.

changes.before: Bring your case forward, says the Lord; present anything strong that you have, says the King of Jacob.
changes.after: Bring your case forward, says the Lord; present anything you may have, says the King of Jacob.
changes.reason: In si quid forte habetis, forte is the adverb “perhaps” (Douay “if perhaps you have any thing”), not fortis “strong”; “anything strong” imports the Hebrew’s “strong arguments” reading.

changes.before: Look, they have become like stubble; fire has burned them. They will not deliver themselves from the power of the flame. These are no coals for warming themselves, no hearth to sit beside.
changes.after: Look, they have become like stubble; fire has burned them. They will not deliver themselves from the power of the flame. There are no coals to warm them, no hearth to sit beside.
changes.reason: Non sunt prunæ quibus calefiant says there will be no coals for them to warm themselves at; “These are no coals” follows the Hebrew image of the consuming fire rather than the Latin.

changes.before: You neither heard nor knew, nor was your ear opened long ago. For I know that you will act treacherously, and I have called you a transgressor from the womb.
changes.after: You neither heard nor knew, nor was your ear opened long ago. For I know that you will surely act treacherously, and I have called you a transgressor from the womb.
changes.reason: Prævaricans prævaricaberis doubles the verb for emphasis (Douay “transgressing thou wilt transgress”); the plain “you will act treacherously” drops it, unlike “Gaudens gaudebo” in 61:10, which the column renders “greatly rejoice”.

changes.before: For who will pity you, Jerusalem, or grieve for you? Who will go to ask about your welfare?
changes.after: For who will pity you, Jerusalem, or grieve for you? Who will go to plead for your peace?
changes.reason: Ad rogandum pro pace tua means going to entreat on behalf of Jerusalem’s peace (Douay “to pray for thy peace”), not to inquire after her welfare, which is the Hebrew idiom rather than the Vulgate’s.

changes.before: “Therefore, look, this time I will make them know; I will show them My hand and My might, and they will know that My name is the Lord.”
changes.after: “Therefore, look, this time I will show them; I will show them My hand and My might, and they will know that My name is the Lord.”
changes.reason: The Latin deliberately repeats ostendam eis (“I will show them this time, I will show them My hand”), and “make them know” both loses that repetition and anticipates the closing et scient.

changes.before: Thus says the Lord: “Go and obtain a potter's earthenware jar from the elders of the people and the elders of the priests.
changes.after: Thus says the Lord: “Go and get a potter's earthenware jar, and take with you some of the elders of the people and some of the elders of the priests.
changes.reason: A senioribus populi is partitive (Douay “take of the ancients of the people”): the elders are the men who go with Jeremiah in 19:10, whereas “obtain a jar from the elders” makes them the source of the jar.

changes.before: But like the very bad figs, too bad to eat, thus says the Lord: So will I make Zedekiah king of Judah, his rulers, and the remnant of Jerusalem who remain in this city and those who live in the land of Egypt.
changes.after: But like the very bad figs, too bad to eat, thus says the Lord: So will I give up Zedekiah king of Judah, his rulers, and the remnant of Jerusalem who remain in this city and those who live in the land of Egypt.
changes.reason: Sic dabo Sedeciam means “so will I give up Zedekiah” (Douay “so will I give Sedecias”); “make Zedekiah king of Judah” with no complement sounds aloud as if God were making him king.

changes.before: For thus says the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel: Take from My hand this cup of the wine of fury, and give it to all the nations to whom I send you to drink.
changes.after: For thus says the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel: Take from My hand this cup of the wine of fury, and make all the nations to whom I send you drink from it.
changes.reason: Propinabis de illo cunctis gentibus means giving the nations a drink from the cup; “to whom I send you to drink” sounds aloud as if the prophet is sent to drink.

changes.before: I took the cup from the Lord's hand and gave it to all the nations to whom the Lord sent me to drink:
changes.after: I took the cup from the Lord's hand and made all the nations to whom the Lord sent me drink from it:
changes.reason: Propinavi cunctis gentibus means “I gave all the nations to drink”; “sent me to drink” misleads the ear, and the wording now matches the command in 32:15.

changes.before: the prophets who were before me and before you from the beginning prophesied against many lands and great kingdoms of war, affliction, and famine.
changes.after: the prophets who were before me and before you from the beginning prophesied of war, affliction, and famine against many lands and great kingdoms.
changes.reason: De prælio, et de afflictione, et de fame is what the prophets foretold; placed after “kingdoms”, “great kingdoms of war” sounds like a description of the kingdoms.

changes.before: “Thus says the Lord: We have heard a cry of terror, fear, and no peace.
changes.after: “Thus says the Lord: We have heard a cry of terror; there is dread, and no peace.
changes.reason: Vocem terroris audivimus: formido, et non est pax makes formido a separate statement (there is dread), but the current line lists “fear” and “no peace” as things heard, which does not parse aloud.

changes.before: You show mercy to thousands and repay the iniquity of fathers into the laps of their children after them. Most strong, great, and mighty, Your name is the Lord of hosts.
changes.after: You show mercy to thousands and repay the iniquity of fathers into the laps of their children after them. O most strong, great, and mighty One, Your name is the Lord of hosts.
changes.reason: Fortissime, magne, et potens are vocatives addressed to God; read aloud, “Most strong, great, and mighty, Your name…” sounds as if the adjectives describe the name.

changes.before: Johanan son of Kareah, all the commanders of the fighting men, and all the people did not obey the voice of the Lord by remaining in the land of Judah.
changes.after: Johanan son of Kareah, all the commanders of the fighting men, and all the people did not obey the voice of the Lord to remain in the land of Judah.
changes.reason: Ut manerent in terra Juda is what the Lord commanded (to remain); “did not obey … by remaining” can be heard as saying that remaining was the disobedience.

changes.before: A continual allowance of food was given him by the king of Babylon, a daily portion until the day of his death, all the days of his life.
changes.after: His allowance of food, a continual allowance, was given him by the king of Babylon, a daily portion until the day of his death, all the days of his life.
changes.reason: The Latin deliberately repeats cibaria ejus, cibaria perpetua (his provisions, continual provisions), which the current line collapses into one phrase.

changes.before: Their legs were straight legs, and the sole of each foot was like the sole of a calf’s foot, with sparks like the appearance of glowing bronze.
changes.after: Their feet were straight feet, and the sole of each foot was like the sole of a calf’s foot, with sparks like the appearance of glowing bronze.
changes.reason: The Vulgate has pedes eorum, pedes recti (“their feet were straight feet”), and “legs” follows the Hebrew raglayim rather than the Latin, which then speaks of the sole of the foot.

changes.before: As for you, son of man, look, they will put bonds on you and bind you with them, and you will not go out from among them.
changes.after: As for you, son of man, look, bonds have been put upon you, and they will bind you with them, and you will not go out from among them.
changes.reason: Ecce data sunt super te vincula is perfect passive (“bonds have been put upon you”), followed by the future ligabunt; the English turned the completed fact into a future act.

changes.before: I, the Lord, have spoken. When I send the deadly arrows of famine against them, arrows that bring death, which I will send to destroy you, I will heap famine upon you and break the staff of bread among you.
changes.after: I, the Lord, have spoken. When I send the evil arrows of famine against them, arrows that bring death, which I will send to destroy you, I will heap famine upon you and break the staff of bread among you.
changes.reason: Sagittas famis pessimas are “most evil” arrows, and mortiferæ (“that bring death”) follows separately; “deadly … that bring death” drops pessimas and says the same thing twice.

changes.before: Therefore thus says the Lord God: Because you have recalled your iniquity, exposed your transgressions, and made your sins appear in all your thoughts—because, I say, you have recalled them—you will be seized by hand.
changes.after: Therefore thus says the Lord God: Because you have recalled your iniquity and exposed your transgressions, and your sins have appeared in all your thoughts—because, I say, you have recalled them—you will be seized by hand.
changes.reason: Apparuerunt peccata vestra is intransitive (“your sins have appeared”), so “made your sins appear” adds an agency the Latin does not have.

changes.before: as silver, bronze, tin, iron, and lead are gathered into a furnace, so that I may kindle a fire in it to melt them. So I will gather you in My fury and My wrath; I will settle and melt you.
changes.after: as silver, bronze, tin, iron, and lead are gathered into a furnace, so that I may kindle a fire in it to melt them. So I will gather you in My fury and My wrath; I will take My rest and melt you.
changes.reason: Requiescam is “I will rest” (Douay “I will take my rest”); read aloud, “I will settle and melt you” sounds like “settle you,” a different act.

changes.before: They will not lie with the mighty, fallen and uncircumcised, who descended to the underworld with their weapons and placed their swords beneath their heads, their iniquities upon their bones, because they became the terror of the mighty in the land of the living.
changes.after: They will not lie with the mighty, fallen and uncircumcised, who descended to the underworld with their weapons and placed their swords beneath their heads, and whose iniquities were in their bones, because they became the terror of the mighty in the land of the living.
changes.reason: The Vulgate reads fuerunt iniquitates eorum in ossibus eorum (“their iniquities were in their bones”), not “upon”; the verbless phrase also trips the ear.

changes.before: I will raise up renowned growth for them, and they will no longer be diminished by famine in the land or bear the reproach of the nations.
changes.after: I will raise up for them a renowned shoot, and they will no longer be diminished by famine in the land or bear the reproach of the nations.
changes.reason: Germen nominatum is a single named shoot or bud (Douay “a bud of renown”), the Vulgate’s germen image; the mass noun “renowned growth” loses it.

changes.before: Thus says the Lord God: In the fire of My jealousy I have spoken concerning the remaining nations and all Edom, who assigned My land to themselves as an inheritance with joy, with all their heart and soul, and cast it out to devastate it.
changes.after: Therefore thus says the Lord God: In the fire of My jealousy I have spoken concerning the remaining nations and all Edom, who assigned My land to themselves as an inheritance with joy, with all their heart and soul, and cast it out to devastate it.
changes.reason: Restores “Propterea” (therefore), which links this oracle to the preceding charge and was omitted.

changes.before: The Lord said to me, “Son of man, set your heart upon, see with your eyes, and hear with your ears everything I say to you concerning all the rites of the Lord's house and all its laws. Set your heart upon the ways of the temple through all the exits of the sanctuary.
changes.after: The Lord said to me, “Son of man, take it to heart: see with your eyes and hear with your ears everything I say to you concerning all the rites of the Lord's house and all its laws. Set your heart upon the ways of the temple through all the exits of the sanctuary.
changes.reason: “Set your heart upon,” with its object deferred, trips the ear; “pone cor tuum” is rendered as a complete phrase.

changes.before: They will eat the sacrifice, the sin offering, and the guilt offering, and everything vowed in Israel will belong to them.
changes.after: They will eat the victim offered both for sin and for guilt, and everything vowed in Israel will belong to them.
changes.reason: “Victimam et pro peccato et pro delicto” names one victim, for sin and for guilt, not three separate offerings.

changes.before: The king said to them, “I have had a dream, and my mind is troubled because I do not know what I saw.”
changes.after: The king said to them, “I have had a dream, and my mind is so confused that I do not know what I saw.”
changes.reason: Latin ‘mente confusus ignoro’ makes the confusion the cause of not knowing, not the result of it.

changes.before: The decree went out, and the wise men were being killed. Daniel and his companions were also sought to be put to death.
changes.after: The decree went out, and the wise men were being killed. Daniel and his companions were also sought out, to be put to death.
changes.reason: ‘were also sought to be put to death’ trips the ear; keeps the Latin passive ‘quaerebantur … ut perirent’.

changes.before: He will enter prosperous and fruitful cities and do what neither his fathers nor his fathers’ fathers did. He will scatter among them plunder, booty, and riches, and will devise plans against the strongest cities, but only for a time.
changes.after: He will enter prosperous and fruitful cities and do what neither his fathers nor his fathers’ fathers did. He will scatter their plunder, booty, and riches, and will devise plans against the strongest cities, but only for a time.
changes.reason: Latin ‘rapinas, et praedam, et divitias eorum dissipabit’ means scattering their spoil, not distributing it among them (a Hebrew reading).

changes.before: In the womb he supplanted his brother, and in his strength he was set firmly with an angel.
changes.after: In the womb he supplanted his brother, and in his strength he prospered with an angel.
changes.reason: In Vulgate usage directus est means he succeeded or prospered (Douay “he had success with an angel”); “was set firmly” misses this and is unclear aloud.

changes.before: From the power of death I will free them; from death I will redeem them. I will be your death, O death! I will be your bite, O underworld! Consolation is hidden from My eyes.
changes.after: From the hand of death I will free them; from death I will redeem them. I will be your death, O death! I will be your bite, O underworld! Consolation is hidden from My eyes.
changes.reason: The Latin keeps the image de manu mortis (“from the hand of death”), which the column should not flatten to “power” in this well-known verse.

changes.before: Seek the Lord and live, lest the house of Joseph burn like fire and it devour, with no one to extinguish it at Bethel,
changes.after: Seek the Lord and live, lest the house of Joseph burn like fire and it devour, with no one to quench Bethel,
changes.reason: Bethel is the object of extinguat (“none to quench Bethel”), not the place where the fire is put out.

changes.before: who smiles devastation upon the strong and brings destruction upon the powerful.
changes.after: who with a smile brings devastation upon the strong and destruction upon the powerful.
changes.reason: Subridet vastitatem means he brings devastation with a smile (Douay “with a smile bringeth destruction”); “smiles devastation upon” is hard to follow aloud.

changes.before: Now why are you contracted with grief? Have you no king, or has your counselor perished, that pain has seized you like a woman giving birth?
changes.after: Now why are you doubled up with grief? Have you no king, or has your counselor perished, that pain has seized you like a woman giving birth?
changes.reason: Mœrore contraheris pictures being drawn together with grief, matching the labour image of the verse; “contracted with grief” is unclear when heard.

changes.before: The just Lord in her midst will do no iniquity. Morning after morning He will bring His judgment to light and will not be hidden, but the wicked person has known no shame.
changes.after: The just Lord in her midst will do no iniquity. Morning after morning He will bring His judgment to light, and it will not be hidden; but the wicked person has known no shame.
changes.reason: In judicium suum dabit in lucem, et non abscondetur, the subject of abscondetur is the judgment (“it will not be hidden”), not the Lord, so the English should not say that He will not be hidden.

changes.before: Thus says the Lord of hosts: If you walk in My ways and keep My charge, you too will govern My house and keep My courts, and I will give you companions from among those who now stand here.
changes.after: Thus says the Lord of hosts: If you walk in My ways and keep My charge, you too will judge My house and keep My courts, and I will give you companions from among those who now stand here.
changes.reason: The Latin has judicabis domum meam (“you will judge My house”), the priestly office of judging that the Vulgate keeps; “govern” follows the Hebrew-based modern versions rather than the Clementine text.

changes.before: The burden of the word of the Lord concerning Israel. Thus says the Lord, who stretches out heaven, lays the earth's foundations, and forms the human spirit within:
changes.after: The burden of the word of the Lord concerning Israel. Thus says the Lord, who stretches out heaven, lays the earth's foundations, and forms the human spirit within him:
changes.reason: Fingens spiritum hominis in eo means forming man’s spirit within him; the bare “within” at the end of the clause dangles when read aloud.

changes.before: Every husband took up lamentation, and those who sat on the marriage bed mourned.
changes.after: Every husband took up lamentation, and the women who sat on the marriage bed mourned.
changes.reason: Quae sedebant is feminine: the brides are set against every husband, which “those” loses.

changes.before: But as the will in heaven may be, so let it be done.”
changes.after: But whatever the will in heaven may be, so let it be done.”
changes.reason: “As the will in heaven may be” trips the ear; “whatever” carries sicut fuerit voluntas clearly aloud.

changes.before: These men were beforehand wherever the beast was; wherever it went, they went, and did not leave it.
changes.after: These men were there in advance wherever the beast was; wherever it went, they went, and did not leave it.
changes.reason: “Were beforehand” is hard to follow aloud; ante tempus means they were already in position wherever the beast was.

changes.before: For he has restored his brothers and driven Israel's enemies away from them.” They established his freedom, inscribed it on bronze tablets, and placed it among the inscriptions on Mount Zion.
changes.after: For he has restored his brothers and driven Israel's enemies away from them.” They established freedom for him, inscribed it on bronze tablets, and placed it among the inscriptions on Mount Zion.
changes.reason: Statuerunt ei libertatem is dative (freedom established for him), not a freedom belonging to Simon as though he had been unfree.

changes.before: All the people approved the appointment of Simon and acting according to these words.
changes.after: All the people agreed to appoint Simon and to act according to these words.
changes.reason: The mixed noun-and-gerund pairing trips the ear; parallel infinitives follow statuere ... et facere.

changes.before: In accordance with the city's common decree, when the Jews agreed, suspecting nothing because of the peace, they went out into deep water and drowned no fewer than two hundred of them.
changes.after: In accordance with the city's common decree, and with the Jews agreeing and suspecting nothing because of the peace, the people of Joppa went out into deep water and drowned no fewer than two hundred of them.
changes.reason: Submerserunt has the people of Joppa as subject, but read aloud “they went out into deep water and drowned” sounds as if the Jews drowned on their own; naming the Joppites keeps who did what clear.

changes.before: When they had gone nine stadia from there and were making their way toward Timothy, five thousand Arab men and five hundred horsemen engaged him in battle.
changes.after: When they had gone nine stadia from there and were making their way toward Timothy, five thousand Arab men and five hundred horsemen engaged Judas in battle.
changes.reason: Commiserunt cum eo means the Arabs fought Judas, but “him” directly after “toward Timothy” makes listeners hear that the Arabs attacked Timothy.

changes.before: Judas then went out to Carnion, twenty-five thousand having been killed.
changes.after: Judas then went out to Carnion, and twenty-five thousand were killed.
changes.reason: The trailing participle “twenty-five thousand having been killed” is hard to follow aloud; a plain passive clause keeps the Latin’s unstated agent and adds nothing to interfectis viginti quinque millibus.

changes.before: And after they were departed, behold an angel of the Lord appeared in sleep to Joseph, saying: Arise, and take the child and his mother, and fly into Egypt: and be there until I shall tell you. For it will happen that Herod will seek the child to destroy him.
changes.after: And after they were departed, behold an angel of the Lord appeared in sleep to Joseph, saying: Arise, and take the child and his mother, and flee into Egypt: and be there until I shall tell you. For it will happen that Herod will seek the child to destroy him.
changes.reason: Fuge means “flee”; the archaic “fly into Egypt” is heard aloud as flying.

changes.before: Then Herod perceiving that he was deluded by the wise men, was exceeding angry: and sending killed all the menchildren that were in Bethlehem, and in all the borders of it, from two years old and under, according to the time which he had diligently inquired of the wise men.
changes.after: Then Herod perceiving that he had been tricked by the wise men, was exceeding angry: and he sent and killed all the boys that were in Bethlehem, and in all the borders of it, from two years old and under, according to the time which he had diligently inquired of the wise men.
changes.reason: Illusus esset means he had been tricked or mocked (not “deluded”), and the clipped “sending killed all the menchildren” is hard to follow aloud for mittens occidit omnes pueros.

changes.before: But hearing that Archelaus reigned in Judea in the room of Herod his father, he was afraid to go there: and being warned in sleep retired into the quarters of Galilee.
changes.after: But hearing that Archelaus reigned in Judea in place of Herod his father, he was afraid to go there: and being warned in sleep retired into the region of Galilee.
changes.reason: Pro Herode means “in place of Herod” and partes Galilææ the region of Galilee; the archaic “in the room of” and “quarters” mislead a modern listener.

changes.before: Whose fan is in his hand, and he will thoroughly cleanse his floor and gather his wheat into the barn; but the chaff he will burn with unquenchable fire.
changes.after: His winnowing fan is in his hand, and he will thoroughly cleanse his threshing floor and gather his wheat into the barn; but the chaff he will burn with unquenchable fire.
changes.reason: Ventilabrum is a winnowing fan and area a threshing floor; heard aloud, “Whose fan … his floor” suggests a household fan and floor.

changes.before: But John stayed him, saying: I ought to be baptized by you, and do you come to me?
changes.after: But John tried to prevent him, saying: I ought to be baptized by you, and do you come to me?
changes.reason: Prohibebat is a conative imperfect (“tried to prevent”); the archaic “stayed him” is not understood as hindering when heard.

changes.before: And much people followed him from Galilee, and from Decapolis, and from Jerusalem, and from Judea, and from beyond the Jordan.
changes.after: And great crowds followed him from Galilee, and from Decapolis, and from Jerusalem, and from Judea, and from beyond the Jordan.
changes.reason: Turbæ multæ means “great crowds”; the archaic “much people” trips the ear (the same Latin is “great multitudes” in 8:1).

changes.before: And another of his disciples said to him: Lord, suffer me first to go and bury my father.
changes.after: And another of his disciples said to him: Lord, allow me first to go and bury my father.
changes.reason: Permitte means “allow”; “suffer me” is heard today as suffering, not permission.

changes.before: And behold the whole city went out to meet Jesus, and when they saw him, they begged him that he would depart from their coasts.
changes.after: And behold the whole city went out to meet Jesus, and when they saw him, they begged him that he would depart from their territory.
changes.reason: A finibus eorum means from their territory; “coasts” (old sense “borders”) is heard as seashore.

changes.before: Whether is easier, to say, Your sins are forgiven you: or to say, Arise, and walk?
changes.after: Which is easier, to say, Your sins are forgiven you: or to say, Arise, and walk?
changes.reason: Quid est facilius asks “which is easier”; the archaic “Whether is easier” does not parse as a question aloud.

changes.before: Go then and learn what this means, I will have mercy and not sacrifice. For I am not come to call the just, but sinners.
changes.after: Go then and learn what this means, I desire mercy and not sacrifice. For I am not come to call the just, but sinners.
changes.reason: Misericordiam volo means “I desire mercy”; “I will have mercy” is now heard as a future “I will show mercy,” losing the contrast with sacrifice.

changes.before: And nobody puts a piece of raw cloth to an old garment. For it takes away the fullness of it from the garment, and there is made a greater rent.
changes.after: And nobody puts a piece of raw cloth to an old garment. For it takes away the fullness of it from the garment, and a worse tear is made.
changes.reason: Pejor scissura fit means a worse tear is made; “a greater rent” is heard as payment, not a tear.

changes.before: Neither do they put new wine into old bottles. Otherwise the bottles break, and the wine runs out, and the bottles perish. But new wine they put into new bottles: and both are preserved.
changes.after: Neither do they put new wine into old wineskins. Otherwise the wineskins break, and the wine runs out, and the wineskins perish. But new wine they put into new wineskins: and both are preserved.
changes.reason: Utres are skins for wine, and the image of old skins bursting is lost with “bottles.”

changes.before: And when Jesus had come into the house of the ruler, and saw the minstrels and the multitude making a rout, he said:
changes.after: And when Jesus had come into the house of the ruler, and saw the minstrels and the multitude making an uproar, he said:
changes.reason: Turbam tumultuantem is a crowd in uproar; “making a rout” is heard as a defeat.

changes.before: And when the multitude was put forth, he went in, and took her by the hand. And the maid arose.
changes.after: And when the multitude was put forth, he went in, and took her by the hand. And the girl arose.
changes.reason: Puella is the same girl called “the girl” in 9:24; “the maid” is heard as a servant.

changes.before: And when he had come to the house, the blind men came to him. And Jesus says to them, Do you believe, that I can do this to you? They say to him, Yes, Lord.
changes.after: And when he had come to the house, the blind men came to him. And Jesus says to them, Do you believe, that I can do this for you? They say to him, Yes, Lord.
changes.reason: Hoc possum facere vobis is a dative of benefit (“do this for you”); “do this to you” sounds threatening aloud.

changes.before: Woe to you, Corozain, woe to you, Bethsaida: for if in Tyre and Sidon had been wrought the miracles that have been wrought in you, they had long ago repented in sackcloth and ashes.
changes.after: Woe to you, Corozain, woe to you, Bethsaida: for if in Tyre and Sidon had been wrought the miracles that have been wrought in you, they would long ago have repented in sackcloth and ashes.
changes.reason: Olim … pœnitentiam egissent is a contrary-to-fact apodosis; the archaic “they had long ago repented” is heard as a statement that they did repent.

changes.before: And you Capernaum, shall you be exalted up to heaven? you shall go down even to the underworld. For if in Sodom had been wrought the miracles that have been wrought in you, perhaps it had remained to this day.
changes.after: And you Capernaum, shall you be exalted up to heaven? you shall go down even to the underworld. For if in Sodom had been wrought the miracles that have been wrought in you, perhaps it would have remained to this day.
changes.reason: Forte mansissent is contrary-to-fact (“would have remained”); the archaic “had remained” is heard as fact, though Sodom did not remain.

changes.before: And if you knew what this means: I will have mercy, and not sacrifice: you would never have condemned the innocent.
changes.after: And if you knew what this means: I desire mercy, and not sacrifice: you would never have condemned the innocent.
changes.reason: Misericordiam volo means “I desire mercy” (as corrected in 9:13); “I will have mercy” is heard as a future promise.

changes.before: As he was yet speaking to the multitudes, behold his mother and his brothers stood without, seeking to speak to him.
changes.after: As he was yet speaking to the multitudes, behold his mother and his brothers stood outside, seeking to speak to him.
changes.reason: Foris means “outside”; “stood without” is heard as lacking something.

changes.before: And one said to him: Behold your mother and your brothers stand without, seeking you.
changes.after: And one said to him: Behold your mother and your brothers stand outside, seeking you.
changes.reason: Foris means “outside”; “stand without” is heard as lacking something (matching 12:46).

changes.before: And other some fell upon stony ground, where they had not much earth: and they sprung up immediately, because they had no deepness of earth.
changes.after: And others fell upon stony ground, where they had not much earth: and they sprung up immediately, because they had no deepness of earth.
changes.reason: Alia autem ceciderunt is simply “others fell” (as in 13:7 and 13:8); “other some” trips the ear.

changes.before: The Son of Man shall send his angels, and they shall gather out of his kingdom all scandals, and them that work iniquity.
changes.after: The Son of Man shall send his angels, and they shall gather out of his kingdom all causes of stumbling, and them that work iniquity.
changes.reason: Omnia scandala are stumbling blocks (the column renders scandalizare as “stumble” in 5:29, 11:6 and 13:21); “scandals” is heard as public disgrace.

changes.before: But Jesus said to them, They have no need to go: give you them to eat.
changes.after: But Jesus said to them, They have no need to go: you give them to eat.
changes.reason: Date illis vos manducare puts the emphatic vos on the disciples (“you give them”), and the archaic “give you them to eat” sounds aloud as if “you” were the thing given.

changes.before: They answered him: We have not here, but five loaves, and two fishes.
changes.after: They answered him: We have nothing here but five loaves, and two fishes.
changes.reason: Non habemus hic nisi means “we have nothing here except”; the archaic “We have not here, but” is hard to follow when read aloud.

changes.before: But they said: Some John the Baptist, and other some Elijah, and others Jeremiah, or one of the prophets.
changes.after: But they said: Some John the Baptist, and others Elijah, and others Jeremiah, or one of the prophets.
changes.reason: Alii autem Eliam is simply “others Elijah”; the archaic “other some” trips the listener.

changes.before: And Peter taking him, began to rebuke him, saying: Lord, be it far from you, this shall not be to you.
changes.after: And Peter taking him, began to rebuke him, saying: Lord, be it far from you, this shall not happen to you.
changes.reason: Non erit tibi hoc means “this shall not happen to you”; “shall not be to you” is opaque when heard.

changes.before: But I say to you, that Elijah is already come, and they knew him not, But have done to him whatever they had a mind. So also the Son of Man shall suffer from them.
changes.after: But I say to you, that Elijah is already come, and they knew him not, but have done to him whatever they wished. So also the Son of Man shall suffer from them.
changes.reason: Fecerunt in eo quæcumque voluerunt is “did to him whatever they wished”; “whatever they had a mind” is an incomplete idiom aloud (stray capital in mid-sentence also lowered).

changes.before: He said: Yes. And when he had come into the house, Jesus prevented him, saying: What is your opinion, Simon? The kings of the earth, of whom do they receive tribute or custom, of their own children, or of strangers?
changes.after: He said: Yes. And when he had come into the house, Jesus spoke to him first, saying: What is your opinion, Simon? The kings of the earth, of whom do they receive tribute or custom, of their own children, or of strangers?
changes.reason: Prævenit eum means Jesus anticipated Peter; in modern English “prevented him” is heard as “stopped him”, which misleads the listener.

changes.before: Who said to them: All men take not this word, but they to whom it is given.
changes.after: Who said to them: Not all men receive this word, but they to whom it is given.
changes.reason: Non omnes capiunt verbum istud means not everyone can receive (grasp) this saying; “All men take not this word” is ambiguous aloud and obscures capiunt, which recurs as “receive” in 19:12.

changes.before: Then Jesus said to his disciples: Amen, I say to you, that a rich man shall hardly enter into the kingdom of heaven.
changes.after: Then Jesus said to his disciples: Amen, I say to you, that a rich man shall enter into the kingdom of heaven with difficulty.
changes.reason: Dives difficile intrabit means the rich man will enter with difficulty; modern “hardly” is heard as “barely” or “scarcely at all”.

changes.before: When therefore they had come that came about the eleventh hour, they received every man a denarius.
changes.after: When therefore those had come who came about the eleventh hour, they received every man a denarius.
changes.reason: The Latin subject is qui circa undecimam horam venerant; “they had come that came” loses the listener, so the relative clause is attached to “those”.

changes.before: And Jesus answered them: Amen, I say to you, if you shall have faith and stagger not, not only this of the fig tree shall you do, but also if you shall say to this mountain, Take up and cast yourself into the sea, it shall be done.
changes.after: And Jesus answered them: Amen, I say to you, if you shall have faith and do not hesitate, not only this of the fig tree shall you do, but also if you shall say to this mountain, Take up and cast yourself into the sea, it shall be done.
changes.reason: Non hæsitaveritis means “do not hesitate/waver”; the archaic Douay “stagger not” is heard as physical staggering.

changes.before: Again he sent other servants, saying: Tell them that were invited, Behold, I have prepared my dinner: my beeves and fatlings are killed, and all things are ready. Come to the marriage.
changes.after: Again he sent other servants, saying: Tell them that were invited, Behold, I have prepared my dinner: my bulls and fatlings are killed, and all things are ready. Come to the marriage.
changes.reason: Tauri mei are “my bulls”; the archaic plural “beeves” is unfamiliar to listeners.

changes.before: And the rest laid hands on his servants and, having treated them contumeliously, put them to death.
changes.after: And the rest laid hands on his servants and, having treated them shamefully, put them to death.
changes.reason: Contumeliis affectos means treated with insults and outrage; “contumeliously” is too obscure to follow aloud.

changes.before: Then the king said to the waiters: Bind his hands and feet, and cast him into the exterior darkness. There shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth.
changes.after: Then the king said to the attendants: Bind his hands and feet, and cast him into the exterior darkness. There shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth.
changes.reason: Ministris are the king’s attendants; “waiters” sounds like restaurant staff to a modern listener.

changes.before: Saying: The scribes and the Pharisees have sitten on the chair of Moses.
changes.after: Saying: The scribes and the Pharisees have sat on the chair of Moses.
changes.reason: Sederunt is “have sat”; the archaic participle “sitten” trips the ear.

changes.before: And all their works they do for to be seen of men. For they make their phylacteries broad and enlarge their fringes.
changes.after: And all their works they do to be seen by men. For they make their phylacteries broad and enlarge their fringes.
changes.reason: Ut videantur ab hominibus is “so as to be seen by men”; the archaic “for to be seen of men” is awkward aloud.

changes.before: You foolish and blind: for whether is greater, the gold or the temple that sanctifies the gold?
changes.after: You foolish and blind: for which is greater, the gold or the temple that sanctifies the gold?
changes.reason: Quid enim majus est means “which is greater”; archaic “whether” in this sense is heard as introducing a condition.

changes.before: You blind: for whether is greater, the gift or the altar that sanctifies the gift?
changes.after: You blind: for which is greater, the gift or the altar that sanctifies the gift?
changes.reason: Quid enim majus est means “which is greater”, as in 23:17; archaic “whether” in this sense is heard as introducing a condition.

changes.before: And you shall hear of wars and rumours of wars. See that you do not be troubled. For these things must happen: but the end is not yet.
changes.after: And you shall hear of wars and rumours of wars. See that you are not troubled. For these things must happen: but the end is not yet.
changes.reason: Videte ne turbemini; “do not be troubled” after “that you” is ungrammatical and stumbles when read aloud.

changes.before: But pray that your flight do not be in the winter or on the sabbath.
changes.after: But pray that your flight may not be in the winter or on the sabbath.
changes.reason: Ut non fiat fuga vestra is a purpose clause (“that your flight may not be”); “do not be” is ungrammatical aloud.

changes.before: If therefore they shall say to you, Behold he is in the desert: go not out. Behold he is in the closets: believe it not.
changes.after: If therefore they shall say to you, Behold he is in the desert: go not out. Behold he is in the inner rooms: believe it not.
changes.reason: In penetralibus means in the inner rooms of a house; modern “closets” suggests cupboards.

changes.before: But this know you, that, if the goodman of the house knew at what hour the thief would come, he would certainly watch and would not suffer his house to be broken open.
changes.after: But this know you, that, if the master of the house knew at what hour the thief would come, he would certainly watch and would not suffer his house to be broken open.
changes.reason: Paterfamilias is the master of the house (as the column renders it in 20:11); “goodman” is archaic and unclear aloud.

changes.before: But if that evil servant shall say in his heart: My lord is long a coming:
changes.after: But if that evil servant shall say in his heart: My lord is long in coming:
changes.reason: Moram fecit dominus meus venire means the master is delaying his coming; the archaic “long a coming” trips the listener.

changes.before: The lord of that servant shall come in a day that he hopes not and at an hour that he does not know:
changes.after: The lord of that servant shall come on a day that he does not expect and at an hour that he does not know:
changes.reason: Sperare here means “to expect” (in die qua non sperat); “hopes not” suggests the servant’s wishes rather than his expectation.

changes.before: The wise answered, saying: Lest perhaps there do not be enough for us and for you, go rather to them that sell and buy for yourselves.
changes.after: The wise answered, saying: Lest perhaps there may not be enough for us and for you, go rather to them that sell and buy for yourselves.
changes.reason: Ne forte non sufficiat is a subjunctive clause (“lest perhaps there may not be enough”); “there do not be” is ungrammatical aloud.

changes.before: And after a little while, they came that stood by and said to Peter: Surely you also are one of them. For even your speech does discover you.
changes.after: And after a little while, they came that stood by and said to Peter: Surely you also are one of them. For even your speech makes you known.
changes.reason: Loquela tua manifestum te facit means “your speech makes you known”; aloud, “does discover you” now sounds like “finds you” rather than “gives you away.”

changes.before: And he answered him to never a word, so that the governor wondered exceedingly.
changes.after: And he gave him no answer to any word, so that the governor wondered exceedingly.
changes.reason: Non respondit ei ad ullum verbum (“he did not answer him to any word”) is garbled aloud as “answered him to never a word.”

changes.before: But the chief priests and ancients persuaded the people that they should ask Barabbas and make Jesus away.
changes.after: But the chief priests and ancients persuaded the people that they should ask for Barabbas and destroy Jesus.
changes.reason: Ut peterent Barabbam, Jesum vero perderent means they should request Barabbas and destroy Jesus; “ask Barabbas” sounds like questioning him and “make Jesus away” is obsolete.

changes.before: And the governor answered them: Whether will you of the two to be released to you? But they said: Barabbas.
changes.after: And the governor answered them: Which of the two will you have released to you? But they said: Barabbas.
changes.reason: Quem … de duobus asks “which of the two”; the archaic “Whether will you” is heard today as “whether,” not “which.”

changes.before: And when they could not offer him to him for the multitude, they uncovered the roof where he was: and opening it, they let down the bed wherein the man sick of the palsy lay.
changes.after: And when they could not bring him to Jesus because of the multitude, they uncovered the roof where he was: and opening it, they let down the bed wherein the man sick of the palsy lay.
changes.reason: Non possent offerre eum illi præ turba means they could not bring him to Jesus because of the crowd; “offer him to him for the multitude” is unclear aloud.

changes.before: Which Jesus immediately knowing in his spirit that they so thought within themselves, says to them: Why think you these things in your hearts?
changes.after: And immediately Jesus, knowing in his spirit that they so thought within themselves, says to them: Why think you these things in your hearts?
changes.reason: The Latin relative opening (quo statim cognito) gives “Which Jesus … knowing … that they so thought,” a doubled object that is hard to follow aloud; the meaning is unchanged.

changes.before: And when he was passing by, he saw Levi, the son of Alphaeus, sitting at the receipt of custom; and he says to him: Follow me. And rising up, he followed him.
changes.after: And when he was passing by, he saw Levi, the son of Alphaeus, sitting at the tax booth; and he says to him: Follow me. And rising up, he followed him.
changes.reason: Telonium is the toll or tax office; “the receipt of custom” is opaque to a listener, and the next verse already says “tax collectors.”

changes.before: For he healed many, so that they pressed upon him for to touch him, as many as had evils.
changes.after: For he healed many, so that they pressed upon him to touch him, as many as had diseases.
changes.reason: Plagas here means bodily afflictions (the column renders the same word “disease” in 5:34); “had evils” sounds moral when read aloud, and “for to” trips the ear.

changes.before: And he made that twelve should be with him, and that he might send them to preach.
changes.after: And he appointed twelve, that they might be with him, and that he might send them to preach.
changes.reason: Fecit ut essent duodecim cum illo is ungrammatical aloud as “he made that twelve should be”; this keeps both purpose clauses (ut essent … ut mitteret).

changes.before: For there is nothing hid, which shall not be made manifest: neither was it made secret, but that it may come abroad.
changes.after: For there is nothing hid, which shall not be made manifest: neither was it made secret, but that it may come to light.
changes.reason: Ut in palam veniat means “come into the open”; today “come abroad” is heard as going overseas.

changes.before: And he said to them: Take care what you hear. In what measure you shall mete, it shall be measured to you again, and more shall be given to you.
changes.after: And he said to them: Take care what you hear. In what measure you shall measure, it shall be measured to you again, and more shall be given to you.
changes.reason: Mensi fueritis is simply “you measure”; the archaic “mete” trips a listener (the brief’s own example), and the change keeps the Latin’s measure/measured play.

changes.before: And they began to pray him that he would depart from their coasts.
changes.after: And they began to pray him that he would depart from their territory.
changes.reason: Fines means borders or territory; “their coasts” misleads aloud, since the scene is on the seashore.

changes.before: And immediately the fountain of her blood was dried up, and she felt in her body that she was healed of the evil.
changes.after: And immediately the fountain of her blood was dried up, and she felt in her body that she was healed of the disease.
changes.reason: Plaga is her bodily affliction, which the column calls “disease” in 5:34 for the same word; “the evil” sounds moral aloud.

changes.before: And immediately Jesus knowing in himself the virtue that had proceeded from him, turning to the multitude, said: Who has touched my garments?
changes.after: And immediately Jesus knowing in himself the power that had proceeded from him, turning to the multitude, said: Who has touched my garments?
changes.reason: Virtus here is power (the column renders virtutes “mighty works” in 6:2, 6:14); “virtue” is heard today as moral goodness.

changes.before: And rising from there he went into the coasts of Tyre and Sidon: and entering into a house, he would that no one should know it. And he could not be hid.
changes.after: And rising from there he went into the territory of Tyre and Sidon: and entering into a house, he would that no one should know it. And he could not be hid.
changes.reason: Fines means borders or territory, not seacoast; aligned with 7:31 where “coasts of Decapolis” (an inland region) plainly misleads.

changes.before: And again going out of the coasts of Tyre, he came by Sidon to the sea of Galilee, through the midst of the coasts of Decapolis.
changes.after: And again going out of the territory of Tyre, he came by Sidon to the sea of Galilee, through the midst of the territory of Decapolis.
changes.reason: Fines means territory; “the coasts of Decapolis” (an inland region) misleads a listener.

changes.before: And he asked his father: How long time is it since this has happened to him? But he said: From his infancy.
changes.after: And he asked his father: How long is it since this has happened to him? But he said: From his infancy.
changes.reason: Quantum temporis est means “how long is it”; “How long time is it” trips the ear without adding anything.

changes.before: And they came to Capernaum. And when they were in the house, he asked them: What did you treat of in the way?
changes.after: And they came to Capernaum. And when they were in the house, he asked them: What were you discussing in the way?
changes.reason: Quid in via tractabatis asks what they were discussing on the road; “treat of” is obscure when heard aloud.

changes.before: And rising up from there, he comes into the coasts of Judea beyond the Jordan: and the multitude flocked to him again. And as he was accustomed, he taught them again.
changes.after: And rising up from there, he comes into the borders of Judea beyond the Jordan: and the multitude flocked to him again. And as he was accustomed, he taught them again.
changes.reason: In fines Judææ means the territory or borders of Judea; “coasts” now suggests a seashore, which Judea beyond the Jordan does not have.

changes.before: And Jesus looking round about, says to his disciples: How hardly shall they that have riches enter into the kingdom of God!
changes.after: And Jesus looking round about, says to his disciples: How hard it is for them that have riches to enter into the kingdom of God!
changes.reason: Quam difficile means “how hard”; heard today, “how hardly” sounds like “scarcely at all” and muddles the exclamation (10:24 already has “how hard is it”).

changes.before: But it is not so among you: but whoever will be greater shall be your minister.
changes.after: But it is not so among you: but whoever wishes to become greater shall be your minister.
changes.reason: Quicumque voluerit fieri major is about wanting to become greater; heard aloud, “whoever will be greater” sounds like a plain future.

changes.before: And whoever will be first among you shall be the servant of all.
changes.after: And whoever wishes to be first among you shall be the servant of all.
changes.reason: Quicumque voluerit … primus esse is about wanting to be first (as 9:35 “If any man desire to be first”); “whoever will be first” sounds like a prediction.

changes.before: And some of them that stood there said to them: What do you loosing the colt?
changes.after: And some of them that stood there said to them: What are you doing, loosing the colt?
changes.reason: Quid facitis solventes pullum is “What are you doing, untying the colt?”; the Douay “What do you loosing” is hard to follow aloud (11:3 already has “What are you doing?”).

changes.before: And he began to speak to them in parables: A certain man planted a vineyard and made a hedge about it and dug a place for the winefat and built a tower and let it to husbandmen: and went into a far country.
changes.after: And he began to speak to them in parables: A certain man planted a vineyard and made a hedge about it and dug a pit for the winepress and built a tower and let it to husbandmen: and went into a far country.
changes.reason: Fodit lacum is the dug-out vat or pit of the winepress; “winefat” is obsolete and unintelligible to a listener.

changes.before: And at the season he sent to the husbandmen a servant to receive of the husbandmen of the fruit of the vineyard.
changes.after: And at the season he sent to the husbandmen a servant to receive from the husbandmen some of the fruit of the vineyard.
changes.reason: Ut ab agricolis acciperet de fructu vineæ means to receive from the tenants a share of the fruit; the doubled “of … of” is hard to parse aloud.

changes.before: And when they shall lead you and deliver you up, do not be thoughtful beforehand what you shall speak: but whatever shall be given you in that hour, that speak you. For it is not you that speak, but the Holy Spirit.
changes.after: And when they shall lead you and deliver you up, do not think beforehand what you shall speak: but whatever shall be given you in that hour, that speak you. For it is not you that speak, but the Holy Spirit.
changes.reason: Nolite præcogitare means do not premeditate; “be thoughtful” now means “be considerate” and misleads the ear.

changes.before: For there will rise up false Christs and false prophets: and they shall show signs and wonders, to seduce (if it were possible) even the elect.
changes.after: For there will rise up false Christs and false prophets: and they shall show signs and wonders, to deceive (if it were possible) even the elect.
changes.reason: Ad seducendos means to lead astray, rendered “deceive” for the same verb in 13:5–6; modern “seduce” carries a sense the Latin does not have here.

changes.before: But Jesus said: Let her alone. Why do you molest her? She has wrought a good work upon me.
changes.after: But Jesus said: Let her alone. Why do you trouble her? She has wrought a good work upon me.
changes.reason: Quid illi molesti estis means “why are you troubling her”; modern “molest” has a sexual sense that badly misleads when read aloud.

changes.before: And her neighbors and kinsfolks heard that the Lord had showed his great mercy towards her: and they congratulated with her.
changes.after: And her neighbors and kinsfolks heard that the Lord had showed his great mercy towards her: and they congratulated her.
changes.reason: Congratulabantur ei is simply “they congratulated her” (rejoiced with her); “congratulated with her” is not current English and trips the ear.

changes.before: And demanding a writing table, he wrote, saying: John is his name. And they all wondered.
changes.after: And demanding a writing tablet, he wrote, saying: John is his name. And they all wondered.
changes.reason: Pugillaris is a small hand-held writing tablet; “writing table” now suggests a desk.

changes.before: And all they that had heard them laid them up in their heart, saying: What an one, think you, shall this child be? For the hand of the Lord was with him.
changes.after: And all they that had heard them laid them up in their heart, saying: What, do you think, shall this child be? For the hand of the Lord was with him.
changes.reason: Quis, putas, puer iste erit asks what this child will turn out to be; “What an one, think you” is archaic and hard to follow aloud.

changes.before: Now she, at the same hour, coming in, confessed to the Lord: and spoke of him to all that looked for the redemption of Israel.
changes.after: Now she, at the same hour, coming in, gave praise to the Lord: and spoke of him to all that looked for the redemption of Israel.
changes.reason: Confitebatur Domino here means she gave thanks and praise to the Lord (the Greek anthomologeito); “confessed” suggests confessing sins.

changes.before: Under the high priests Annas and Caiaphas: the word of the Lord was made to John, the son of Zechariah, in the desert.
changes.after: Under the high priests Annas and Caiaphas: the word of the Lord came upon John, the son of Zechariah, in the desert.
changes.reason: Factum est verbum Domini super Joannem means the word of the Lord came upon John; “was made to John” is a Latinism that is hard to follow aloud.

changes.before: And the soldiers also asked him, saying: And what shall we do? And he said to them: Do violence to no one, neither calumniate any man; and be content with your pay.
changes.after: And the soldiers also asked him, saying: And what shall we do? And he said to them: Do violence to no one, nor accuse anyone falsely; and be content with your pay.
changes.reason: Calumniam faciatis means to bring false accusations; “calumniate” is obscure when heard.

changes.before: John answered, saying to all: I indeed baptize you with water: but there shall come one mightier than I, the latchet of whose sandals I am not worthy to loose. He shall baptize you with the Holy Spirit and with fire;
changes.after: John answered, saying to all: I indeed baptize you with water: but there shall come one mightier than I, the strap of whose sandals I am not worthy to loose. He shall baptize you with the Holy Spirit and with fire;
changes.reason: Corrigia is the strap of the sandal; “latchet” is archaic Douay wording that a listener will not follow.

changes.before: Whose fan is in his hand: and he will purge his floor and will gather the wheat into his barn: but the chaff he will burn with unquenchable fire.
changes.after: Whose winnowing fan is in his hand: and he will purge his threshing floor and will gather the wheat into his barn: but the chaff he will burn with unquenchable fire.
changes.reason: Ventilabrum and area are the winnowing fan and threshing floor; bare “fan” and “floor” mislead the ear (same fix as Matthew 3:12).

changes.before: And when it was day, going out he went into a desert place: and the multitudes sought him, and came to him. And they stayed him that he should not depart from them.
changes.after: And when it was day, going out he went into a desert place: and the multitudes sought him, and came to him. And they tried to hold him back, that he should not depart from them.
changes.reason: Detinebant (imperfect) means they were trying to hold him back; archaic “stayed him” is misheard (same fix as Matthew 3:14).

changes.before: Now when he had ceased to speak, he said to Simon: Launch out into the deep and let down your nets for a draught.
changes.after: Now when he had ceased to speak, he said to Simon: Launch out into the deep and let down your nets for a catch.
changes.reason: In capturam means for a catch; “draught” sounds like “draft” when read aloud.

changes.before: For he was wholly astonished, and all that were with him, at the draught of the fishes which they had taken.
changes.after: For he was wholly astonished, and all that were with him, at the catch of fish which they had taken.
changes.reason: In captura piscium is the catch of fish; “draught of the fishes” is opaque aloud (matches 5:4).

changes.before: And after these things, he went forth and saw a tax collector named Levi, sitting at the receipt of custom: and he said to him: Follow me.
changes.after: And after these things, he went forth and saw a tax collector named Levi, sitting at the tax booth: and he said to him: Follow me.
changes.reason: Telonium is the tax-collector’s booth; “receipt of custom” is archaic and unclear to a listener.

changes.before: And no one puts new wine into old bottles: otherwise the new wine will break the bottles; and it will be spilled and the bottles will be lost.
changes.after: And no one puts new wine into old wineskins: otherwise the new wine will break the wineskins; and it will be spilled and the wineskins will be lost.
changes.reason: Utres are wineskins, and the image of skins bursting is lost with “bottles” (same fix as Matthew 9:17).

changes.before: But new wine must be put into new bottles: and both are preserved.
changes.after: But new wine must be put into new wineskins: and both are preserved.
changes.reason: Utres novos are new wineskins; keeps the image consistent with 5:37 and Matthew 9:17.

changes.before: And no one drinking old has immediately a mind to new: for he says: The old is better.
changes.after: And no one drinking old wine immediately wants new: for he says: The old is better.
changes.reason: Statim vult novum means immediately wants the new; “has a mind to” trips the ear, and “wine” (understood from 5:37–38) makes “old” intelligible aloud.

changes.before: And all the multitude sought to touch him: for virtue went out from him and healed all.
changes.after: And all the multitude sought to touch him: for power went out from him and healed all.
changes.reason: Virtus here is power (as the column renders it in 4:36 and 5:17); “virtue” now means moral goodness and misleads a listener.

changes.before: Bless them that curse you and pray for them that calumniate you.
changes.after: Bless them that curse you and pray for them that falsely accuse you.
changes.reason: Calumniantibus vos means those who falsely accuse you; “calumniate” is obscure when heard.

changes.before: Give to everyone that asks you: and of him that takes away your goods, ask them not again.
changes.after: Give to everyone that asks you: and of him that takes away your goods, do not ask them back.
changes.reason: Ne repetas means do not demand them back; “ask them not again” sounds like “do not ask a second time.”

changes.before: Give: and it shall be given to you: good measure and pressed down and shaken together and running over shall they give into your bosom. For with the same measure that you shall mete, it shall be measured to you again.
changes.after: Give: and it shall be given to you: good measure and pressed down and shaken together and running over shall they give into your bosom. For with the same measure with which you measure, it shall be measured to you again.
changes.reason: Qua mensi fueritis means with which you measure; archaic “mete” trips a listener and loses the measure/measured echo of the Latin.

changes.before: And why see you the mote in your brother’s eye: but the beam that is in your own eye you consider not?
changes.after: And why do you see the speck in your brother’s eye: but the beam that is in your own eye you do not consider?
changes.reason: Festuca is a speck or splinter; “mote” and the inverted “see you … consider not” are hard to follow aloud.

changes.before: Or how can you say to your brother: Brother, let me pull the mote out of your eye, when you yourself see not the beam in your own eye? Hypocrite, cast first the beam out of your own eye: and then shall you see clearly to take out the mote from your brother’s eye.
changes.after: Or how can you say to your brother: Brother, let me pull the speck out of your eye, when you yourself see not the beam in your own eye? Hypocrite, cast first the beam out of your own eye: and then shall you see clearly to take out the speck from your brother’s eye.
changes.reason: Festuca rendered “speck” as in 6:41; “mote” is archaic and unclear aloud.

changes.before: And when he had heard of Jesus, he sent to him the ancients of the Jews, desiring him to come and heal his servant.
changes.after: And when he had heard of Jesus, he sent to him the elders of the Jews, desiring him to come and heal his servant.
changes.reason: Seniores Judaeorum are the elders of the Jews; “ancients” suggests people of long ago.

changes.before: And other some fell upon a rock. And as soon as it was sprung up, it withered away, because it had no moisture.
changes.after: And other seed fell upon a rock. And as soon as it was sprung up, it withered away, because it had no moisture.
changes.reason: Aliud (another part of the seed) rendered “other some” trips the ear (cf. Matthew 13:5 fix); “other seed” keeps the singular.

changes.before: And other some fell among thorns. And the thorns growing up with it, choked it.
changes.after: And other seed fell among thorns. And the thorns growing up with it, choked it.
changes.reason: Same as 8:6: aliud is other seed; “other some” is archaic and awkward aloud.

changes.before: And other some fell upon good ground and, being sprung up, yielded fruit a hundredfold. Saying these things, he cried out: He that has ears to hear, let him hear.
changes.after: And other seed fell upon good ground and, being sprung up, yielded fruit a hundredfold. Saying these things, he cried out: He that has ears to hear, let him hear.
changes.reason: Same as 8:6: aliud is other seed; “other some” is archaic and awkward aloud.

changes.before: And his mother and brothers came to him: and they could not come at him for the crowd.
changes.after: And his mother and brothers came to him: and they could not get to him because of the crowd.
changes.reason: Non poterant adire eum prae turba means they could not reach him because of the crowd; “come at him for the crowd” is misleading aloud.

changes.before: And it was told him: Your mother and your brothers stand without, desiring to see you.
changes.after: And it was told him: Your mother and your brothers stand outside, desiring to see you.
changes.reason: Stant foris means stand outside; “stand without” is heard as “lacking” (same fix as Matthew 12:47).

changes.before: The demons therefore went out of the man and entered into the swine. And the herd ran violently down a steep place into the lake and were stifled.
changes.after: The demons therefore went out of the man and entered into the swine. And the herd ran violently down a steep place into the lake and were drowned.
changes.reason: Suffocatus est in stagnum describes the herd choked in the lake, i.e. drowned; “stifled” is unclear aloud.

changes.before: And Jesus said: Somebody has touched me; for I know that virtue has gone out from me.
changes.after: And Jesus said: Somebody has touched me; for I know that power has gone out from me.
changes.reason: Virtutem de me exiisse means power went out from him (as in 6:19); “virtue” misleads a modern listener.

changes.before: By some that John had risen from the dead: but by other some, that Elijah had appeared: and by others, that one of the old prophets had risen again.
changes.after: By some that John had risen from the dead: but by some, that Elijah had appeared: and by others, that one of the old prophets had risen again.
changes.reason: A quibusdam vero means by some (others); archaic “other some” trips the ear (cf. Matthew 16:14 fix).

changes.before: But he said to them: Give you them to eat. And they said: We have no more than five loaves and two fishes; unless perhaps, we should go and buy food for all this multitude.
changes.after: But he said to them: You give them to eat. And they said: We have no more than five loaves and two fishes; unless perhaps, we should go and buy food for all this multitude.
changes.reason: Vos date illis manducare puts the emphatic vos first; “Give you them” is heard as an odd command (same fix as Matthew 14:16).

changes.before: Saying: The Son of Man must suffer many things and be rejected by the ancients and chief priests and scribes and be killed and the third day rise again.
changes.after: Saying: The Son of Man must suffer many things and be rejected by the elders and chief priests and scribes and be killed and the third day rise again.
changes.reason: Senioribus are the elders; “ancients” suggests people of long ago (matches 7:3).

changes.before: And lo, a spirit seizes him, and he suddenly cries out, and he throws him down and tears him, so that he foams; and bruising him, he hardly departs from him.
changes.after: And lo, a spirit seizes him, and he suddenly cries out, and it throws him down and tears him, so that he foams; and bruising him, it hardly departs from him.
changes.reason: The subject of elidit, dissipat and discedit is the spirit; with “he” for both spirit and boy a listener cannot tell who throws whom down.

changes.before: But he said to another: Follow me. And he said: Lord, suffer me first to go and to bury my father.
changes.after: But he said to another: Follow me. And he said: Lord, allow me first to go and to bury my father.
changes.reason: Permitte mihi means allow me; “suffer me” is misheard today (same fix as Matthew 8:21).

changes.before: And the Lord answered to her: Martha, Martha, you are careful and are troubled about many things:
changes.after: And the Lord answered to her: Martha, Martha, you are anxious and are troubled about many things:
changes.reason: Sollicita es means you are anxious; “careful” now means cautious and misleads the listener.

changes.before: And he was casting out a devil: and the same was dumb. And when he had cast out the devil, the dumb spoke: and the multitudes, were in admiration at it.
changes.after: And he was casting out a devil: and the same was dumb. And when he had cast out the devil, the dumb spoke: and the multitudes marvelled.
changes.reason: Admiratae sunt turbae means the crowds marvelled; “were in admiration” suggests admiring and the stray comma breaks the sentence aloud.

changes.before: And it happened, as he spoke these things, a certain woman from the crowd, lifting up her voice, said to him: Blessed is the womb that bore you and the paps that gave you suck.
changes.after: And it happened, as he spoke these things, a certain woman from the crowd, lifting up her voice, said to him: Blessed is the womb that bore you and the breasts that nursed you.
changes.reason: Ubera quae suxisti are the breasts that nursed him; “paps that gave you suck” is archaic and jarring aloud.

changes.before: And you yourselves like to men who wait for their lord, when he shall return from the wedding; that when he comes and knocks, they may open to him immediately.
changes.after: And be you yourselves like men who wait for their lord, when he shall return from the wedding; that when he comes and knocks, they may open to him immediately.
changes.reason: The clause has no verb and “like to men” trips the ear; the implied imperative (sitis/estote, continuing sint in 12:35) is supplied as “be you”.

changes.before: Blessed are those servants whom the Lord, when he comes, shall find watching. Amen, I say to you that he will gird himself and make them sit down to table and passing will minister to them.
changes.after: Blessed are those servants whom the lord, when he comes, shall find watching. Amen, I say to you that he will gird himself and make them sit down to table and, passing by, will minister to them.
changes.reason: Dominus here is the master of the parable (the column writes “his lord” in 12:43), so capital “Lord” wrongly names God; “passing will minister” is also hard to follow aloud for transiens ministrabit.

changes.before: Be then also ready: for at what hour you think not the Son of Man will come.
changes.after: Be then also ready: for at an hour you do not think, the Son of Man will come.
changes.reason: Read aloud, “you think not the Son of Man will come” sounds as if they think he will not come; qua hora non putatis means at an hour they do not expect.

changes.before: But if that servant shall say in his heart: My lord is long a coming; and shall begin to strike the men-servants and maid-servants, and to eat and to drink and be drunk:
changes.after: But if that servant shall say in his heart: My lord delays his coming; and shall begin to strike the men-servants and maid-servants, and to eat and to drink and be drunk:
changes.reason: “Is long a coming” is archaic and trips the ear; moram facit … venire means he delays his coming.

changes.before: The lord of that servant will come in the day that he hopes not, and at the hour that he does not know: and shall separate him and shall appoint him his portion with unbelievers.
changes.after: The lord of that servant will come on the day that he does not expect, and at the hour that he does not know: and shall separate him and shall appoint him his portion with unbelievers.
changes.reason: Sperare here means to expect, not to hope; “hopes not” misleads a modern listener, and the line parallels “the hour that he does not know”.

changes.before: And he said to the dresser of the vineyard: Behold, for these three years I come seeking fruit on this fig tree and I find none. Cut it down therefore. Why burdens it the ground?
changes.after: And he said to the dresser of the vineyard: Behold, for these three years I come seeking fruit on this fig tree and I find none. Cut it down therefore. Why does it even take up the ground?
changes.reason: “Why burdens it the ground?” is inverted and hard to follow; ut quid etiam terram occupat asks why it even occupies the ground.

changes.before: And if happily it bear fruit: but if not, then after that you shall cut it down.
changes.after: And if it bears fruit, well: but if not, then after that you shall cut it down.
changes.reason: “Happily” in the old sense of “perhaps” is heard today as “joyfully”; siquidem fecerit fructum is an elliptical “if it bears fruit, well and good”.

changes.before: Nevertheless, I must walk to-day and to-morrow and the day following, because it cannot be that a prophet perish, out of Jerusalem.
changes.after: Nevertheless, I must walk to-day and to-morrow and the day following, because it cannot be that a prophet perish outside Jerusalem.
changes.reason: Extra Jerusalem means outside Jerusalem; the comma and “out of” make the line sound as if the prophet perishes on leaving Jerusalem.

changes.before: And he that invited you and him, come and say to you: Give this man place. And then you begin with shame to take the lowest place.
changes.after: And he that invited you and him should come and say to you: Give this man place. And then you would begin with shame to take the lowest place.
changes.reason: The subjunctives (dicat, incipias) continue the “lest” of 14:8; as written the sentence has no grammatical verb and reads like a command when spoken.

changes.before: And the Lord said to the servant: Go out into the highways and hedges, and compel them to come in, that my house may be filled.
changes.after: And the lord said to the servant: Go out into the highways and hedges, and compel them to come in, that my house may be filled.
changes.reason: Dominus is the householder of the parable (called “his lord” and “the master of the house” in 14:21), so capital “Lord” wrongly names God.

changes.before: If then you have not been faithful in the unjust mammon, who will trust you with that which is the true?
changes.after: If then you have not been faithful in the unjust mammon, who will trust you with that which is true?
changes.reason: “That which is the true” is ungrammatical aloud; quod verum est is simply “that which is true”.

changes.before: He said to them, “You justify yourselves before people, but God knows your hearts. What people hold in high esteem is an abomination before God.
changes.after: He said to them: You are the ones who justify yourselves before people, but God knows your hearts; for what people hold in high esteem is an abomination before God.
changes.reason: The row opened a quotation mark that never closes (the column uses colon-introduced speech), dropped the emphatic Vos estis qui (“you are the ones who”) and the causal quia (“for”).

changes.before: And besides all this, between us and you, there is fixed a great chaos: so that they who would pass from here to you cannot, nor from there come here.
changes.after: And besides all this, between us and you, there is fixed a great chasm: so that they who would pass from here to you cannot, nor from there come here.
changes.reason: Latin chaos here means a gulf or chasm; in modern English “chaos” means disorder and misleads the listener.

changes.before: And if he sin against you seven times in a day, and seven times in a day be converted to you, saying: I repent: forgive him.
changes.after: And if he sin against you seven times in a day, and seven times in a day turn back to you, saying: I repent: forgive him.
changes.reason: Conversus fuerit ad te means turning back to the one wronged; “be converted to you” is heard today as religious conversion to a person.

changes.before: But which of you, having a servant ploughing or feeding cattle, will say to him, when he has come from the field: Immediately go. Sit down to table.
changes.after: But which of you, having a servant ploughing or feeding cattle, will say to him, when he has come from the field: Come at once, sit down to table.
changes.reason: Statim transi, recumbe invites the servant straight to the table; “Immediately go.” sounds like a dismissal when read aloud.

changes.before: And Jesus seeing him become sorrowful, said: How hardly shall they that have riches enter into the kingdom of God!
changes.after: And Jesus seeing him become sorrowful, said: How hard it is for them that have riches to enter into the kingdom of God!
changes.reason: “How hardly” is now heard as “scarcely at all”; quam difficile means how difficult it is.

changes.before: Saying: Go into the town which is over against you, at your entering into which you shall find the colt of a donkey tied, on which no one ever has sitten: loose him and bring him here.
changes.after: Saying: Go into the town which is over against you, at your entering into which you shall find the colt of a donkey tied, on which no one has ever sat: loose him and bring him here.
changes.reason: “Sitten” is an obsolete form that trips the ear; cui nemo umquam hominum sedit is simply “on which no one has ever sat”.

changes.before: Lay it up therefore in your hearts, not to meditate before how you shall answer:
changes.after: Lay it up therefore in your hearts, not to prepare beforehand how you shall answer:
changes.reason: Præmeditari means to prepare in advance; “meditate before” is unclear when heard.

changes.before: But Jesus answered: Suffer you thus far. And when he had touched his ear, he healed him.
changes.after: But Jesus answered: Allow it thus far. And when he had touched his ear, he healed him.
changes.reason: “Suffer you” in the old sense of “permit” is heard today as “endure”; sinite usque huc means allow it up to this point (the column renders sinite as “allow” in 18:16).

changes.before: And Herod with his army set him at nought and mocked him, putting on him a white garment: and sent him back to Pilate.
changes.after: And Herod with his army treated him with contempt and mocked him, putting on him a white garment: and sent him back to Pilate.
changes.reason: Sprevit means he despised him; “set him at nought” is archaic and hard to follow aloud.

changes.before: No, nor Herod neither. For, I sent you to him: and behold, nothing worthy of death is done to him.
changes.after: No, nor Herod neither. For, I sent you to him: and behold, nothing worthy of death has been done by him.
changes.reason: Actum est ei is a dative of agent (done by him, i.e. Jesus has done nothing deserving death); “done to him” reverses the sense when heard.

changes.before: But they were instant with loud voices, requiring that he might be crucified. And their voices prevailed.
changes.after: But they pressed on with loud voices, demanding that he be crucified. And their voices prevailed.
changes.reason: Instabant … postulantes: “were instant … requiring” is obsolete Douay English that a listener will not follow.

changes.before: And as they were afraid and bowed down their countenance towards the ground, they said to them: Why seek you the living with the dead?
