changes.after: And as they were afraid and bowed down their countenance towards the ground, they said to them: Why do you seek the living with the dead?
changes.reason: Modern word order for Quid quæritis; “Why seek you” trips the ear.

changes.before: And the one of them, whose name was Cleophas, answered him: Are you only a stranger in Jerusalem, and have not known the things that have been done there in these days?
changes.after: And the one of them, whose name was Cleophas, answered him: Are you the only stranger in Jerusalem who has not known the things that have been done there in these days?
changes.reason: Tu solus peregrinus es means “are you alone a stranger,” but modern “only a stranger” is heard as “merely a stranger.”

changes.before: Yes and certain women also of our company affrighted us who, before it was light, were at the tomb,
changes.after: Yes and certain women also of our company frightened us who, before it was light, were at the tomb,
changes.reason: Terruerunt nos; “affrighted” is archaic and stumbles when read aloud.

changes.before: His mother says to the waiters: Whatever he shall say to you, do you.
changes.after: His mother says to the waiters: Whatever he shall say to you, do it.
changes.reason: Facite after quodcumque dixerit vobis: the Douay “do ye” rendered “do you” sounds unfinished aloud; “do it” keeps the command.

changes.before: And when the chief steward had tasted the water made wine and knew not from where it was, but the waiters knew who had drawn the water: the chief steward calls the bridegroom,
changes.after: And when the chief steward had tasted the water made wine and knew not from where it was, but the waiters who had drawn the water knew: the chief steward calls the bridegroom,
changes.reason: Ministri autem sciebant, qui hauserant aquam means the waiters who had drawn the water knew (where the wine came from), not that they knew who drew it.

changes.before: But Jesus did not trust himself to them: for that he knew all men,
changes.after: But Jesus did not trust himself to them: because he knew all men,
changes.reason: Eo quod = because; “for that” is archaic and confusing aloud.

changes.before: He that has received his testimony has set to his seal that God is true.
changes.after: He that has received his testimony has set his seal to this, that God is true.
changes.reason: Signavit, quia Deus verax est: “set to his seal” is obsolete phrasing that a listener cannot parse.

changes.before: And he was of necessity to pass through Samaria.
changes.after: And he had to pass through Samaria.
changes.reason: Oportebat autem eum transire: “was of necessity to pass” is awkward archaic English; “had to” carries oportebat plainly.

changes.before: Jesus answered to her: Whoever drinks of this water shall thirst again: but he that shall drink of the water that I will give him shall not thirst forever.
changes.after: Jesus answered to her: Whoever drinks of this water shall thirst again: but he that shall drink of the water that I will give him shall never thirst.
changes.reason: Non sitiet in æternum means he will never thirst; “shall not thirst forever” is heard as a thirst that merely will not last.

changes.before: And immediately his disciples came. And they wondered that he talked with the woman. Yet no one said: What seek you? Or: Why talk you with her?
changes.after: And immediately his disciples came. And they wondered that he talked with the woman. Yet no one said: What do you seek? Or: Why do you talk with her?
changes.reason: Modern word order for Quid quæris … Quid loqueris; “Why talk you” trips the ear.

changes.before: Do not you say: There are yet four months, and then the harvest comes? Behold, I say to you, lift up your eyes, and see the countries. For they are white already to harvest.
changes.after: Do not you say: There are yet four months, and then the harvest comes? Behold, I say to you, lift up your eyes, and see the fields. For they are white already to harvest.
changes.reason: Regiones albæ ad messem are tracts of farmland; modern “countries” suggests nations and blurs the harvest image.

changes.before: The ruler says to him: Lord, come down before that my son die.
changes.after: The ruler says to him: Lord, come down before my son dies.
changes.reason: Priusquam moriatur: “before that my son die” is archaic and stumbles aloud.

changes.before: The father therefore knew that it was at the same hour that Jesus said to him: Your son lives. And himself believed, and his whole house.
changes.after: The father therefore knew that it was at the same hour that Jesus said to him: Your son lives. And he himself believed, and his whole house.
changes.reason: Credidit ipse: the subjectless “And himself believed” is hard to follow aloud.

changes.before: Him when Jesus had seen lying, and knew that he had been now a long time, he says to him: Will you be made well?
changes.after: When Jesus had seen him lying there, and knew that he had been so for a long time now, he says to him: Will you be made well?
changes.reason: The Latin word order (Hunc … cum vidisset) copied into English, with “had been now a long time,” cannot be followed aloud.

changes.before: There is another that bears witness of me: and I know that the witness which he bears witness of me is true.
changes.after: There is another that bears witness of me: and I know that the witness which he bears of me is true.
changes.reason: Testimonium quod perhibet de me has the noun once; “witness which he bears witness” doubles it and trips the ear.

changes.before: Philip answered him: Two hundred pennyworth of bread is not sufficient for them that everyone may take a little.
changes.after: Philip answered him: Two hundred denarii’s worth of bread is not sufficient for them, that everyone may take a little.
changes.reason: Ducentorum denariorum: “pennyworth” misstates the sum to a modern ear; the Latin names denarii.

changes.before: When therefore the multitude saw that Jesus was not there, nor his disciples, they took shipping and came to Capernaum, seeking for Jesus.
changes.after: When therefore the multitude saw that Jesus was not there, nor his disciples, they got into the boats and came to Capernaum, seeking for Jesus.
changes.reason: Ascenderunt in naviculas; “took shipping” is archaic and obscure aloud, and the boats were just mentioned in 6:23.

changes.before: And when they had found him on the other side of the sea, they said to him: Rabbi, when came you here?
changes.after: And when they had found him on the other side of the sea, they said to him: Rabbi, when did you come here?
changes.reason: Modern word order for Quando huc venisti; “when came you” trips the ear.

changes.before: It is written in the prophets: And they shall all be taught of God. Everyone that has heard of the Father and has learned comes to me.
changes.after: It is written in the prophets: And they shall all be taught of God. Everyone that has heard from the Father and has learned comes to me.
changes.reason: Audivit a Patre means heard from the Father (taught by him, as the quotation says); “heard of” is heard as merely hearing about him.

changes.before: If any man will do the will of him, he shall know of the doctrine, whether it be of God, or whether I speak of myself.
changes.after: If any man is willing to do his will, he shall know of the doctrine, whether it be of God, or whether I speak of myself.
changes.reason: Si quis voluerit … facere stresses willingness to do God’s will; “will do” is heard as a plain future and loses voluerit.

changes.before: Why seek you to kill me? The multitude answered: You have a devil. Who seeks to kill you?
changes.after: Why do you seek to kill me? The multitude answered: You have a devil. Who seeks to kill you?
changes.reason: Modern word order for Quid me quæritis interficere; “Why seek you” trips the ear.

changes.before: The Jews therefore said among themselves: Whither will he go, that we shall not find him? Will he go to the dispersed among the Gentiles and teach the Gentiles?
changes.after: The Jews therefore said among themselves: Where will he go, that we shall not find him? Will he go to the dispersed among the Gentiles and teach the Gentiles?
changes.reason: Quo hic iturus est: “Whither” is archaic; “where” is the plain spoken equivalent.

changes.before: Jesus therefore said to them: When you shall have lifted up, the Son of Man, then shall you know that I am he and that I do nothing of myself. But as the Father has taught me, these things I speak.
changes.after: Jesus therefore said to them: When you shall have lifted up the Son of Man, then shall you know that I am he and that I do nothing of myself. But as the Father has taught me, these things I speak.
changes.reason: The stray comma splits verb from object (exaltaveritis Filium hominis) and misleads when read aloud.

changes.before: You are of your father the devil: and the desires of your father you will do. He was a murderer from the beginning: and he stood not in the truth, because truth is not in him. When he speaks a lie, he speaks of his own: for he is a liar, and the father of it.
changes.after: You are of your father the devil: and the desires of your father you want to do. He was a murderer from the beginning: and he stood not in the truth, because truth is not in him. When he speaks a lie, he speaks of his own: for he is a liar, and the father of it.
changes.reason: Vultis facere expresses will/desire, which modern “you will do” turns into a simple future.

changes.before: Which of you shall convince me of sin? If I say the truth to you, why do you not believe me?
changes.after: Which of you shall convict me of sin? If I say the truth to you, why do you not believe me?
changes.reason: Arguet means to convict or prove guilty; modern “convince” means persuade.

changes.before: Now we know that God does not hear sinners: but if a man be a server of God and does his will, him he hears.
changes.after: Now we know that God does not hear sinners: but if a man be a worshipper of God and does his will, him he hears.
changes.reason: Dei cultor is a worshipper of God; “server” is unclear aloud.

changes.before: The thief comes not, but for to steal and to kill and to destroy. I am come that they may have life and may have it more abundantly.
changes.after: The thief comes only to steal and to kill and to destroy. I am come that they may have life and may have it more abundantly.
changes.reason: Archaic “comes not, but for to” trips the ear; nisi ut = only to.

changes.before: The Jews answered him: For a good work we stone you not, but for blasphemy: and because that you, being a man, make yourself God.
changes.after: The Jews answered him: For a good work we stone you not, but for blasphemy: and because you, being a man, make yourself God.
changes.reason: Archaic “because that” smoothed; meaning unchanged.

changes.before: Martha therefore said to Jesus: Lord, if you had been here, my brother had not died.
changes.after: Martha therefore said to Jesus: Lord, if you had been here, my brother would not have died.
changes.reason: Archaic conditional “had not died” can be heard as a statement; non fuisset mortuus is counterfactual.

changes.before: When Mary therefore had come where Jesus was, seeing him, she fell down at his feet and says to him: Lord, if you had been here, my brother had not died.
changes.after: When Mary therefore had come where Jesus was, seeing him, she fell down at his feet and says to him: Lord, if you had been here, my brother would not have died.
changes.reason: Archaic conditional “had not died” can be heard as a statement; non esset mortuus is counterfactual.

changes.before: Jesus says: Take away the stone. Martha, the sister of him that was dead, says to him: Lord, by this time he smells, for he is now of four days.
changes.after: Jesus says: Take away the stone. Martha, the sister of him that was dead, says to him: Lord, by this time he smells, for he has now been dead four days.
changes.reason: Quatriduanus est: “is now of four days” is opaque aloud.

changes.before: The chief priests, therefore, and the Pharisees gathered a council and said: What do we, for this man does many miracles?
changes.after: The chief priests, therefore, and the Pharisees gathered a council and said: What are we doing, for this man does many miracles?
changes.reason: Quid facimus? as a live question; archaic “What do we” trips the ear.

changes.before: They sought therefore for Jesus; and they discoursed one with another, standing in the temple: What think you that he is not come to the festival day? And the chief priests and Pharisees had given a commandment that, if any man knew where he was, he should tell, that they might apprehend him.
changes.after: They sought therefore for Jesus; and they discoursed one with another, standing in the temple: What do you think, that he has not come to the festival day? And the chief priests and Pharisees had given a commandment that, if any man knew where he was, he should tell, that they might apprehend him.
changes.reason: Quid putatis, quia non venit: the archaic question is hard to follow aloud.

changes.before: The multitude therefore gave testimony, which was with him, when he called Lazarus out of the grave and raised him from the dead.
changes.after: The multitude therefore, which was with him when he called Lazarus out of the grave and raised him from the dead, gave testimony.
changes.reason: The relative clause was detached from “multitude” and read as if it referred to the testimony.

changes.before: Peter says to him: You shall never wash my feet, Jesus answered him: If I wash you not, you shall have no part with me.
changes.after: Peter says to him: You shall never wash my feet. Jesus answered him: If I wash you not, you shall have no part with me.
changes.reason: The comma made “Jesus” sound like Peter’s vocative; the Latin begins a new sentence (Respondit ei Jesus).

changes.before: Jesus says to him: He that is washed needs not but to wash his feet, but is clean wholly. And you are clean, but not all.
changes.after: Jesus says to him: He that is washed needs only to wash his feet, but is wholly clean. And you are clean, but not all.
changes.reason: Non indiget nisi ut: “needs not but to” and “clean wholly” trip the ear.

changes.before: At present I tell you, before it happen: that when it will happen, you may believe that I am he.
changes.after: At present I tell you, before it happens: that when it has happened, you may believe that I am he.
changes.reason: Priusquam fiat … cum factum fuerit: the second verb is future perfect (“has happened”), and “before it happen” is ungrammatical aloud.

changes.before: Jesus answered: He it is to whom I shall reach bread dipped. And when he had dipped the bread, he gave it to Judas Iscariot, the son of Simon.
changes.after: Jesus answered: It is he to whom I shall hand the bread I have dipped. And when he had dipped the bread, he gave it to Judas Iscariot, the son of Simon.
changes.reason: Cui intinctum panem porrexero: “reach bread dipped” is opaque aloud.

changes.before: And now I have told you before it happen: that when it will happen, you may believe.
changes.after: And now I have told you before it happens: that when it has happened, you may believe.
changes.reason: Priusquam fiat … cum factum fuerit: the second verb is future perfect (“has happened”), and “before it happen” is ungrammatical aloud.

changes.before: And when he has come, he will convince the world of sin and of justice and of judgment.
changes.after: And when he has come, he will convict the world of sin and of justice and of judgment.
changes.reason: Arguet means to convict or prove guilty; modern “convince” means persuade.

changes.before: And now glorify you me, O Father, with yourself, with the glory which I had, before the world was, with you.
changes.after: And now glorify me, O Father, with yourself, with the glory which I had, before the world was, with you.
changes.reason: “Glorify you me” is unsayable; the vocative already carries tu.

changes.before: But Peter stood at the door without. The other disciple therefore, who was known to the high priest, went out and spoke to the portress and brought in Peter.
changes.after: But Peter stood outside at the door. The other disciple therefore, who was known to the high priest, went out and spoke to the portress and brought in Peter.
changes.reason: Ad ostium foris: archaic “without” (= outside) is misheard as “lacking”.

changes.before: And the soldiers platting a crown of thorns, put it upon his head: and they put on him a purple garment.
changes.after: And the soldiers weaving a crown of thorns, put it upon his head: and they put on him a purple garment.
changes.reason: Plectentes: archaic “platting” is unclear aloud (sounds like “plotting”).

changes.before: Simon Peter says to them: I go a fishing. They say to him: We also come with you. And they went forth and entered into the boat: and that night they caught nothing.
changes.after: Simon Peter says to them: I am going fishing. They say to him: We also come with you. And they went forth and entered into the boat: and that night they caught nothing.
changes.reason: Vado piscari is a plain “I am going fishing”; the archaic “I go a fishing” trips the ear when read aloud.

changes.before: Him therefore when Peter had seen, he says to Jesus: Lord, and what shall this man do?
changes.after: When Peter therefore had seen him, he says to Jesus: Lord, and what shall this man do?
changes.reason: The fronted object (“Him therefore when Peter had seen”) copies Latin word order and is hard to follow aloud; the sense of Hunc ergo cum vidisset Petrus is unchanged.

changes.before: And when they had come into the upper room, they went up where abode Peter and John, James and Andrew, Philip and Thomas, Bartholomew and Matthew, James of Alphaeus and Simon Zelotes and Jude of James.
changes.after: And when they had come into the upper room, they went up to where they were staying: Peter and John, James and Andrew, Philip and Thomas, Bartholomew and Matthew, James of Alphaeus and Simon Zelotes and Jude of James.
changes.reason: “where abode Peter and John …” inverts the verb before a long list of names and is hard to follow aloud; ubi manebant is simply “where they were staying.”

changes.before: And praying, they said: You, Lord, who know the heart of all men, show whether of these two you have chosen,
changes.after: And praying, they said: You, Lord, who know the heart of all men, show which one of these two you have chosen,
changes.reason: Archaic “whether of these two” (= which of the two) misleads a modern listener; ostende quem elegeris ex his duobus unum is “show which one of these two you have chosen.”

changes.before: Whom God has raised up, having loosed the sorrows of the underworld, as it was impossible that he should be holden by it.
changes.after: Whom God has raised up, having loosed the sorrows of the underworld, as it was impossible that he should be held by it.
changes.reason: Archaic participle “holden” trips the ear; teneri is simply “be held.”

changes.before: But Peter seeing, answered to the people: You men of Israel, why wonder you at this? Or why look you upon us, as if by our strength or power we had made this man to walk?
changes.after: But Peter seeing, answered to the people: You men of Israel, why do you wonder at this? Or why do you look upon us, as if by our strength or power we had made this man to walk?
changes.reason: The inverted “why wonder you … why look you” is hard to follow aloud; quid miramini … quid intuemini are ordinary questions.

changes.before: Then the twelve, calling together the multitude of the disciples, said: It is not reason that we should leave the word of God and serve tables.
changes.after: Then the twelve, calling together the multitude of the disciples, said: It is not right that we should leave the word of God and serve tables.
changes.reason: Non est æquum means “it is not right/fitting”; the archaic idiom “it is not reason” is unclear to a modern listener.

changes.before: Then he went out of the land of the Chaldeans and dwelt in Charan. And from there, after his father was dead, he removed him into this land, wherein you now dwell.
changes.after: Then he went out of the land of the Chaldeans and dwelt in Charan. And from there, after his father was dead, God removed him into this land, wherein you now dwell.
changes.reason: The subject of transtulit is God (from 7:2–3), but after “he went out … and dwelt” a listener hears “he removed him” as Abraham moving someone; naming God keeps the Latin sense clear aloud.

changes.before: And they were translated into Sichem and were laid in the tomb that Abraham bought for a sum of money of the sons of Hemor, the son of Sichem.
changes.after: And they were carried over into Sichem and were laid in the tomb that Abraham bought for a sum of money of the sons of Hemor, the son of Sichem.
changes.reason: Translati sunt means “were carried across”; read aloud, “translated” now suggests language, not the moving of the bodies.

changes.before: And Philip running there, heard him reading the prophet Isaiah. And he said: Think you that you understand what you read?
changes.after: And Philip running there, heard him reading the prophet Isaiah. And he said: Do you think that you understand what you read?
changes.reason: The archaic inversion “Think you that …” trips the ear; Putasne intelligis quæ legis is an ordinary question.

changes.before: And when he had come into Jerusalem, he essayed to join himself to the disciples: and they all were afraid of him, not believing that he was a disciple.
changes.after: And when he had come into Jerusalem, he tried to join himself to the disciples: and they all were afraid of him, not believing that he was a disciple.
changes.reason: Tentabat se jungere means “he tried to join”; the archaic “essayed” is obscure when heard.

changes.before: Saying: Why did you go in to men uncircumcised and did eat with them?
changes.after: Saying: Why did you go in to men uncircumcised and eat with them?
changes.reason: “Why did you go in … and did eat” is ungrammatical and trips the ear; the second verb (manducasti) shares the same question.

changes.before: And they conversed there in the church a whole year: and they taught a great multitude, so that at Antioch the disciples were first named Christians.
changes.after: And they stayed there in the church a whole year: and they taught a great multitude, so that at Antioch the disciples were first named Christians.
changes.reason: Conversati sunt means “they lived/stayed” (Douay’s old sense of “conversed”); a modern listener hears “conversed” as “talked.”

changes.before: And seeing that it pleased the Jews, he proceeded to take up Peter also. Now it was in the days of the Azymes.
changes.after: And seeing that it pleased the Jews, he proceeded to take up Peter also. Now it was in the days of Unleavened Bread.
changes.reason: Dies Azymorum is the feast of Unleavened Bread; the Douay loanword “Azymes” is opaque to a listener.

changes.before: And when he had apprehended him, he cast him into prison, delivering him to four files of soldiers, to be kept, intending, after the pasch, to bring him forth to the people.
changes.after: And when he had apprehended him, he cast him into prison, delivering him to four files of soldiers, to be kept, intending, after the Passover, to bring him forth to the people.
changes.reason: Post Pascha means after the Passover; the archaic Douay “pasch” trips the ear.

changes.before: And Barnabas and Saul, returned from Jerusalem, having fulfilled their ministry, taking with them John who was surnamed Mark.
changes.after: And Barnabas and Saul returned from Jerusalem, having fulfilled their ministry, taking with them John who was surnamed Mark.
changes.reason: Reversi sunt is the main verb, but the comma makes “returned” sound like a participle and leaves the verse without a main clause when read aloud.

changes.before: And when John was fulfilling his course, he said: I am not he whom you think me to be. But behold, there comes one after me, whose sandals of his feet I am not worthy to loose.
changes.after: And when John was fulfilling his course, he said: I am not he whom you think me to be. But behold, there comes one after me, the sandals of whose feet I am not worthy to loose.
changes.reason: Cujus non sum dignus calceamenta pedum solvere: “whose sandals of his feet” is ungrammatical aloud; “the sandals of whose feet” keeps the Latin image.

changes.before: This same God has fulfilled to our children, raising up Jesus, as in the second psalm also is written: You are my Son: this day have I begotten you.
changes.after: God has fulfilled this same promise to our children, raising up Jesus, as in the second psalm also is written: You are my Son: this day have I begotten you.
changes.reason: Hanc Deus adimplevit means God has fulfilled this (promise, from 13:32); read aloud, “This same God” is heard as describing God rather than as the object.

changes.before: But the Jews stirred up religious and honorable women and the chief men of the city: and raised persecution against Paul and Barnabas: and cast them out of their coasts.
changes.after: But the Jews stirred up religious and honorable women and the chief men of the city: and raised persecution against Paul and Barnabas: and cast them out of their borders.
changes.reason: De finibus suis means from their territory; the Douay “coasts” now suggests the seashore.

changes.before: And when there was an assault made by the Gentiles and the Jews with their rulers, to use them contumeliously and to stone them:
changes.after: And when there was an assault made by the Gentiles and the Jews with their rulers, to treat them shamefully and to stone them:
changes.reason: Ut contumeliis afficerent means to treat them with insults; “contumeliously” is obscure when heard.

changes.before: And let us out themselves. And the serjeants told these words to the magistrates. And they were afraid: hearing that they were Romans.
changes.after: And let them bring us out themselves. And the serjeants told these words to the magistrates. And they were afraid: hearing that they were Romans.
changes.reason: Et ipsi nos ejiciant means “and let them themselves bring us out”; “let us out themselves” sounds like “let us go out ourselves.”

changes.before: Declaring and insinuating that the Christ was to suffer and to rise again from the dead; and that this is Jesus Christ, whom I preach to you.
changes.after: Explaining and making known that the Christ was to suffer and to rise again from the dead; and that this is Jesus Christ, whom I preach to you.
changes.reason: Adaperiens et insinuans means opening up and making known; in modern English “insinuating” suggests sly hinting.

changes.before: And they stirred up the people: and the rulers of the city, hearing these things,
changes.after: And they stirred up the people and the rulers of the city, who heard these things.
changes.reason: Principes is a second object of concitaverunt (they stirred up the people and the rulers), but the colon makes the rulers the subject of 17:9.

changes.before: so that they might seek God, in case they might reach out for him or find him, though he is not far from any one of us.
changes.after: so that they might seek God, if perhaps they might reach out for him or find him, though he is not far from any one of us.
changes.reason: Si forte attrectent means “if perhaps they might feel for him”; modern “in case” means “as a precaution against.”

changes.before: And it happened, while Apollos was at Corinth, that Paul, having passed through the upper coasts, came to Ephesus and found certain disciples.
changes.after: And it happened, while Apollos was at Corinth, that Paul, having passed through the upper regions, came to Ephesus and found certain disciples.
changes.reason: Peragratis superioribus partibus means the upper (inland) parts; the Douay “coasts” now suggests the seashore.

changes.before: But as soon as they perceived him to be a Jew, all with one voice, for the space of about two, hours, cried out: Great is Diana of the Ephesians!
changes.after: But as soon as they perceived him to be a Jew, all with one voice, for the space of about two hours, cried out: Great is Diana of the Ephesians!
changes.reason: A stray comma splits “two hours” (quasi per horas duas) and would make a reader pause mid-phrase.

changes.before: But we sailed from Philippi after the days of the azymes and came to them to Troas in five days, where we abode seven days.
changes.after: But we sailed from Philippi after the days of Unleavened Bread and came to them to Troas in five days, where we abode seven days.
changes.reason: Post dies azymorum means after the days of Unleavened Bread; the Douay “azymes” is opaque to a listener.

changes.before: Take these and sanctify yourself with them: and bestow on them, that they may shave their heads. And all will know that the things which they have heard of you are false: but that you yourself also walk keeping the law.
changes.after: Take these and sanctify yourself with them: and pay their expenses, that they may shave their heads. And all will know that the things which they have heard of you are false: but that you yourself also walk keeping the law.
changes.reason: Impende in illis means spend on them, i.e. bear the cost of their offerings; “bestow on them” leaves the listener asking what is bestowed.

changes.before: And the tribune answered: I obtained the being free of this city with a great sum. And Paul said: But I was born so.
changes.after: And the tribune answered: I obtained this citizenship with a great sum. And Paul said: But I was born so.
changes.reason: Civilitatem hanc consecutus sum means “I obtained this citizenship” (Roman, from 22:27); “the being free of this city” is opaque and suggests Jerusalem.

changes.before: And Paul, looking upon the council, said: Men, brothers, I have conversed with all good conscience before God until this present day.
changes.after: And Paul, looking upon the council, said: Men, brothers, I have lived with all good conscience before God until this present day.
changes.reason: Conversatus sum means I have conducted myself or lived; modern “conversed” means talked.

changes.before: Then Paul said to him: God shall strike you, you whitewashed wall. For, sit you to judge me according to the law and, contrary to the law, command me to be struck?
changes.after: Then Paul said to him: God shall strike you, you whitewashed wall. And do you sit to judge me according to the law and, contrary to the law, command me to be struck?
changes.reason: Et tu sedens judicas me is a question introduced by et; “For, sit you to judge me” is archaic word order that is hard to follow aloud.

changes.before: But Festus answered: That Paul was kept in Cæsarea: and that he himself would very shortly depart there.
changes.after: But Festus answered: That Paul was kept in Cæsarea: and that he himself would very shortly go there.
changes.reason: Se maturius profecturum means he would set out shortly (for Caesarea); “depart there” sounds like leaving from Caesarea.

changes.before: Which also I did at Jerusalem: and many of the saints did I shut up in prison, having received authority of the chief priests. And when they were put to death, I brought the sentence.
changes.after: Which also I did at Jerusalem: and many of the saints did I shut up in prison, having received authority of the chief priests. And when they were put to death, I cast my vote.
changes.reason: Detuli sententiam means Paul gave his vote or verdict against them; “brought the sentence” is obscure when heard.

changes.before: And when we were all fallen down on the ground, I heard a voice speaking to me in the Hebrew tongue: Saul, Saul, why persecute you me? It is hard for you to kick against the goad.
changes.after: And when we were all fallen down on the ground, I heard a voice speaking to me in the Hebrew tongue: Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me? It is hard for you to kick against the goad.
changes.reason: The inverted “why persecute you me” trips the ear; modern word order keeps the Latin quid me persequeris exactly.

changes.before: Believe you the prophets, O king Agrippa? I know that you believe.
changes.after: Do you believe the prophets, O king Agrippa? I know that you believe.
changes.reason: The inverted question “Believe you the prophets” is awkward aloud; Credis is a plain question.

changes.before: And running under a certain island that is called Cauda, we had much work to come by the boat.
changes.after: And running under a certain island that is called Cauda, we were scarcely able to secure the boat.
changes.reason: Potuimus vix obtinere scapham means they could scarcely secure the boat; “come by the boat” now sounds like visiting it.

changes.before: And we, being mightily tossed with the tempest, the next day they lightened the ship.
changes.after: And as we were mightily tossed with the tempest, the next day they lightened the ship.
changes.reason: The Latin ablative absolute (nobis jactatis) left “we” hanging without a verb; making it a clause lets the sentence be followed aloud.

changes.before: But as the shipmen sought to fly out of the ship, having let down the boat into the sea, under color, as though they would have cast anchors out of the forepart of the ship,
changes.after: But as the shipmen sought to fly out of the ship, having let down the boat into the sea, under pretext, as though they would have cast anchors out of the forepart of the ship,
changes.reason: Sub obtentu means under a pretext; the archaic “under color” is unclear to a listener.

changes.before: And when we were fallen into a place where two seas met, they run the ship aground. And the forepart indeed, sticking fast, remained unmoveable: but the hinder part was broken with the violence of the sea.
changes.after: And when we were fallen into a place where two seas met, they ran the ship aground. And the forepart indeed, sticking fast, remained unmoveable: but the hinder part was broken with the violence of the sea.
changes.reason: Impegerunt is perfect; the archaic past “run” sounds like a present tense in a past narrative.

changes.before: And as they liked not to have God in their knowledge, God delivered them up to a reprobate sense, to do those things which are not convenient.
changes.after: And as they liked not to have God in their knowledge, God delivered them up to a reprobate sense, to do those things which are not fitting.
changes.reason: Quae non conveniunt means what is not fitting; “not convenient” now means merely inconvenient.

changes.before: And think you this, O man, that judge them who do such things and do the same, that you shall escape the judgment of God?
changes.after: And do you think this, O man, that judge them who do such things and do the same, that you shall escape the judgment of God?
changes.reason: Existimas is a plain question; the inverted “think you this” is hard to follow aloud.

changes.before: Or despise you the riches of his goodness and patience and longsuffering? Do you not know that the benignity of God leads you to repentance?
changes.after: Or do you despise the riches of his goodness and patience and longsuffering? Do you not know that the benignity of God leads you to repentance?
changes.reason: Contemnis is a plain question; the inverted “despise you” trips the ear.

changes.before: For it is not he is a Jew, who is so outwardly: nor is that circumcision which is outwardly in the flesh.
changes.after: For he is not a Jew who is one outwardly: nor is that circumcision which is outwardly in the flesh.
changes.reason: Non enim qui in manifesto, Judaeus est; the Douay word order “it is not he is a Jew” is garbled when read aloud.

changes.before: As David also calls the blessedness of a man to whom God counts justice without works:
changes.after: As David also speaks of the blessedness of a man to whom God counts justice without works:
changes.reason: Dicit beatitudinem means David speaks of (declares) the blessedness; “calls the blessedness” has no clear sense aloud.

changes.before: Neither yield you your members as instruments of iniquity to sin: but present yourselves to God, as those that are alive from the dead; and your members as instruments of justice to God.
changes.after: Neither yield your members as instruments of iniquity to sin: but present yourselves to God, as those that are alive from the dead; and your members as instruments of justice to God.
changes.reason: The pleonastic “yield you your members” trips the ear; neque exhibeatis membra vestra needs no extra pronoun.

changes.before: I speak an human thing, because of the infirmity of your flesh. For as you have yielded your members to serve uncleanness and iniquity, to iniquity: so now yield your members to serve justice, to sanctification.
changes.after: I speak in human terms, because of the infirmity of your flesh. For as you have yielded your members to serve uncleanness and iniquity, to iniquity: so now yield your members to serve justice, to sanctification.
changes.reason: Humanum dico means Paul speaks in a human way; “an human thing” is archaic and unclear aloud.

changes.before: But I see another law in my members, fighting against the law of my mind and captivating me in the law of sin that is in my members.
changes.after: But I see another law in my members, fighting against the law of my mind and making me captive to the law of sin that is in my members.
changes.reason: Captivantem me means taking me captive; “captivating” now means charming and reverses the image for a listener.

changes.before: Not as though the word of God has miscarried. For all are not Israelites that are of Israel.
changes.after: Not as though the word of God has failed. For all are not Israelites that are of Israel.
changes.reason: Exciderit means has fallen or failed; “miscarried” now suggests a lost pregnancy.

changes.before: And not only she. But when Rebecca also had conceived at once of Isaac our father.
changes.after: And not only she. But when Rebecca also had conceived by one union with Isaac our father.
changes.reason: Ex uno concubitu means from one union (one father for both twins), the point of Paul’s argument; “at once” reads as “immediately”.

changes.before: For God has concluded all in unbelief, that he may have mercy on all.
changes.after: For God has shut up all in unbelief, that he may have mercy on all.
changes.reason: Conclusit means shut up or enclosed; “concluded” now means finished or inferred.

changes.before: For princes are not a terror to the good work, but to the evil. Will you then not be afraid of the power? Do that which is good: and you shall have praise from the same.
changes.after: For princes are not a terror to the good work, but to the evil. Do you wish, then, not to be afraid of the power? Do that which is good: and you shall have praise from the same.
changes.reason: Vis autem non timere potestatem asks whether one wants to be free of fear; “Will you then not be afraid” is heard as “won’t you be afraid”, the opposite sense.

changes.before: Let us walk honestly, as in the day: not in rioting and drunkenness, not in chambering and impurities, not in contention and envy.
changes.after: Let us walk honestly, as in the day: not in rioting and drunkenness, not in debauchery and impurities, not in contention and envy.
changes.reason: In cubilibus refers to sexual licence; the archaic “chambering” is unintelligible to most listeners.

changes.before: But you, why judge you your brother? Or you, why do you despise your brother? For we shall all stand before the judgment seat of Christ.
changes.after: But you, why do you judge your brother? Or you, why do you despise your brother? For we shall all stand before the judgment seat of Christ.
changes.reason: Quid judicas is a plain question; the inverted “why judge you” trips the ear and clashes with “why do you despise” in the same verse.

changes.before: By the virtue of signs and wonders, in the power of the Holy Spirit, so that from Jerusalem round about, as far as to Illyricum, I have replenished the gospel of Christ.
changes.after: By the virtue of signs and wonders, in the power of the Holy Spirit, so that from Jerusalem round about, as far as to Illyricum, I have fully preached the gospel of Christ.
changes.reason: “Replenished the gospel” is opaque aloud; repleverim Evangelium means Paul has fully proclaimed it.

changes.before: Who also will confirm you to the end without crime, in the day of the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ.
changes.after: Who also will confirm you to the end without blame, in the day of the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ.
changes.reason: Sine crimine means without charge or reproach; “without crime” suggests criminality to a listener.

changes.before: That, as it is written: He that boasts may glory in the Lord.
changes.after: That, as it is written: He that glories, let him glory in the Lord.
changes.reason: Restores the jussive glorietur and the Latin’s deliberate repetition gloriatur … glorietur.

changes.before: But the sensual man perceives not these things that are of the Spirit of God. For it is foolishness to him: and he cannot understand, because it is spiritually examined.
changes.after: But the natural man perceives not these things that are of the Spirit of God. For it is foolishness to him: and he cannot understand, because it is spiritually examined.
changes.reason: Animalis homo is the merely natural man (as 15:44 renders animale); “sensual” now implies lust.

changes.before: For, whereas there is among you envying and contention, are you not carnal and walk you not according to man?
changes.after: For, whereas there is among you envying and contention, are you not carnal and do you not walk according to man?
changes.reason: Inverted archaic question is hard to follow aloud.

changes.before: For we are God’s coadjutors. You are God’s husbandry: you are God’s building.
changes.after: For we are God’s helpers. You are God’s husbandry: you are God’s building.
changes.reason: “Coadjutors” trips the ear; adjutores is rendered “helpers” elsewhere in the column (Rom 16:3, 16:9).

changes.before: But these things, brothers, I have in a figure transferred to myself and to Apollos, for your sakes: that in us you may learn that one do not be puffed up against the other for another, above that which is written.
changes.after: But these things, brothers, I have in a figure transferred to myself and to Apollos, for your sakes: that in us you may learn that one be not puffed up against the other for another, above that which is written.
changes.reason: “Do not be” after “that” is ungrammatical in English; restores the subjunctive.

changes.before: It is absolutely heard that there is sexual immorality among you and such sexual immorality as the like is not among the heathens: that one should have his father’s wife.
changes.after: It is actually reported that there is sexual immorality among you and such sexual immorality as the like is not among the heathens: that one should have his father’s wife.
changes.reason: Omnino auditur: “absolutely heard” is unidiomatic and unclear aloud.

changes.before: Purge out the old leaven, that you may be a new paste, as you are unleavened. For Christ our pasch is sacrificed.
changes.after: Purge out the old leaven, that you may be new dough, as you are unleavened. For Christ our pasch is sacrificed.
changes.reason: Conspersio is dough; “paste” obscures the leaven image.

changes.before: And such some of you were. But you are washed: but you are sanctified: but you are justified: in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ and the Spirit of our God.
changes.after: And such some of you were. But you are washed: but you are sanctified: but you are justified: in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ and in the Spirit of our God.
changes.reason: Latin repeats in (et in Spiritu); without it the Spirit can be misheard as part of “the name of”.

changes.before: Meat for the belly and the belly for the foods: but God shall destroy both it and them. But the body is not for sexual immorality, but for the Lord: and the Lord for the body.
changes.after: Food for the belly and the belly for food: but God shall destroy both it and them. But the body is not for sexual immorality, but for the Lord: and the Lord for the body.
changes.reason: Esca … escis is one word; “meat” now means flesh and the mismatch confuses the ear.

changes.before: Fly sexual immorality. Every sin that a man does is without the body: but he that commits sexual immorality sins against his own body.
changes.after: Flee sexual immorality. Every sin that a man does is without the body: but he that commits sexual immorality sins against his own body.
changes.reason: Archaic “fly” (fugite) is heard as the modern verb; “flee” is the sense.

changes.before: For if a man see him that has knowledge sit at table in the idol’s temple, shall not his conscience, being weak, be emboldened to eat those things which are sacrificed to idols?
changes.after: For if a man see him that has knowledge sit at table in the idol’s temple, shall not his conscience, being weak, be built up to eat those things which are sacrificed to idols?
changes.reason: Ædificabitur is Paul’s ironic “built up”, echoing 8:1 “love builds up”; “emboldened” loses the image.

changes.before: To them that are under the law, as if I were under the law, (whereas myself was not under the law,) that I might gain them that were under the law. To them that were without the law, as if I were without the law, (whereas I was not without the law of God, but was in the law of Christ,) that I might gain them that were without the law.
changes.after: To them that are under the law, as if I were under the law, (whereas I myself was not under the law,) that I might gain them that were under the law. To them that were without the law, as if I were without the law, (whereas I was not without the law of God, but was in the law of Christ,) that I might gain them that were without the law.
changes.reason: Supplies the missing subject so the parenthesis is grammatical aloud.

changes.before: Let no temptation take hold on you, but such as is human. And God is faithful, who will not suffer you to be tempted above that which you are able: but will make also with temptation issue, that you may be able to bear it.
changes.after: Let no temptation take hold on you, but such as is human. And God is faithful, who will not suffer you to be tempted above that which you are able: but will also make with the temptation a way out, that you may be able to bear it.
changes.reason: “Make also with temptation issue” is unintelligible aloud; proventum is the way out.

changes.before: Therefore, my dearly beloved, fly from the service of idols.
changes.after: Therefore, my dearly beloved, flee from the service of idols.
changes.reason: Archaic “fly” (fugite) is heard as the modern verb; “flee” is the sense.

changes.before: Whatever is sold in the shambles, eat: asking no question for conscience’ sake.
changes.after: Whatever is sold in the meat market, eat: asking no question for conscience’ sake.
changes.reason: “Shambles” (macellum) is obsolete in this sense and misleads a listener.

changes.before: For if a woman do not be covered, let her be shorn. But if it be a shame to a woman to be shorn or made bald, let her cover her head.
changes.after: For if a woman be not covered, let her be shorn. But if it be a shame to a woman to be shorn or made bald, let her cover her head.
changes.reason: “Do not be” is ungrammatical; restores the subjunctive (si non velatur).

changes.before: Does not even nature itself teach you that a man indeed, if he nourish his hair, it is a shame to him?
changes.after: Does not even nature itself teach you that a man indeed, if he let his hair grow long, it is a shame to him?
changes.reason: Comam nutriat means to grow the hair long; “nourish his hair” misleads aloud.

changes.before: But if a woman nourish her hair, it is a glory to her; for her hair is given to her for a covering.
changes.after: But if a woman let her hair grow long, it is a glory to her; for her hair is given to her for a covering.
changes.reason: Comam nutriat means to grow the hair long; “nourish her hair” misleads aloud.

changes.before: For everyone takes before his own supper to eat. And one indeed is hungry and another is drunk.
changes.after: For everyone takes his own supper beforehand to eat. And one indeed is hungry and another is drunk.
changes.reason: Præsumit means takes beforehand; “takes before his own supper” is misheard as a preposition.

changes.before: But while we are judged, we are chastised by the Lord, that we do not be condemned with this world.
changes.after: But while we are judged, we are chastised by the Lord, that we may not be condemned with this world.
changes.reason: “Do not be” after “that” is ungrammatical; restores the purpose clause.

changes.before: Are all apostles? Are all prophets? Are all doctors?
changes.after: Are all apostles? Are all prophets? Are all teachers?
changes.reason: Doctores is rendered “teachers” in 12:28; “doctors” is now heard as physicians.

changes.before: Do not be seduced: Evil communications corrupt good manners.
changes.after: Do not be seduced: Evil conversations corrupt good morals.
changes.reason: Colloquia mala / mores: “communications” and “manners” have shifted meaning and mislead aloud.

changes.before: And if it be meet that I also go, they shall go with me.
changes.after: And if it is fitting that I also go, they shall go with me.
changes.reason: Dignum fuerit means “it is fitting”; the archaic “meet” is easily misheard aloud.

changes.before: For I will not see you now by the way: for I trust that I shall abide with you some time, if the Lord permit.
changes.after: For I do not wish to see you now only in passing: for I trust that I shall abide with you some time, if the Lord permit.
changes.reason: Nolo … videre in transitu means “I do not wish to see you just in passing,” not a flat future refusal to see them.

changes.before: For a great door and evident is opened to me: and many adversaries.
changes.after: For a great and evident door is opened to me: and there are many adversaries.
changes.reason: The inverted Douay order (“a great door and evident”) and the verbless last clause trip the ear; the Latin sense is unchanged.

changes.before: Let no one therefore despise him: but conduct you him on his way in peace, that he may come to me. For I look for him with the brothers.
changes.after: Let no one therefore despise him: but bring him on his way in peace, that he may come to me. For I look for him with the brothers.
changes.reason: “Conduct you him” is hard to follow aloud; deducite simply means bring or escort him on his way.

changes.before: For our glory is this: the testimony of our conscience, that in simplicity of heart and sincerity of God, and not in carnal wisdom, but in the grace of God, we have conversed in this world: and more abundantly towards you.
changes.after: For our glory is this: the testimony of our conscience, that in simplicity of heart and sincerity of God, and not in carnal wisdom, but in the grace of God, we have conducted ourselves in this world: and more abundantly towards you.
changes.reason: Conversati sumus means “we have conducted ourselves”; modern “conversed” is heard as “talked.”

changes.before: For to this end also did I write, that I may know the experiment of you, whether you be obedient in all things.
changes.after: For to this end also did I write, that I may know the proof of you, whether you be obedient in all things.
changes.reason: Experimentum here is the proof or testing of their obedience; “experiment” misleads a modern listener.

changes.before: But we renounce the hidden things of dishonesty, not walking in craftiness nor adulterating the word of God: but by manifestation of the truth commending ourselves to every man’s conscience, in the sight of God.
changes.after: But we renounce the hidden things of shame, not walking in craftiness nor adulterating the word of God: but by manifestation of the truth commending ourselves to every man’s conscience, in the sight of God.
changes.reason: Occulta dedecoris are the hidden things of shame or disgrace; modern “dishonesty” is heard as lying.

changes.before: Insomuch, that we desired Titus, that, as he had begun, so also he would finish among you this same grace.
changes.after: Insomuch, that we asked Titus, that, as he had begun, so also he would finish among you this same grace.
changes.reason: Rogaremus Titum means “we asked Titus”; “desired” in its archaic sense of “requested” is misheard today.

changes.before: For we forecast what may be good, not only before God but also before men.
changes.after: For we take thought for what is good, not only before God but also before men.
changes.reason: Providemus bona means “we take thought for (provide for) what is good”; “forecast” suggests prediction.

changes.before: Therefore I thought it necessary to desire the brothers that they would go to you before and prepare this blessing before promised, to be ready, so as a blessing, not as greed.
changes.after: Therefore I thought it necessary to ask the brothers that they would go to you before and prepare this blessing before promised, to be ready, so as a blessing, not as greed.
changes.reason: Rogare fratres means to ask the brothers; archaic “desire” is misheard aloud.

changes.before: I have taken from other churches, receiving wages of them for your ministry.
changes.after: I have robbed other churches, receiving wages of them for your ministry.
changes.reason: Expoliavi is “I despoiled, robbed,” Paul’s deliberately strong image, which “taken from” softens away.

changes.before: And, when I was present with you and wanted, I was chargeable to no one: for that which was wanting to me, the brothers supplied who came from Macedonia. And in all things I have kept myself from being burthensome to you: and so I will keep myself.
changes.after: And, when I was present with you and in want, I was a burden to no one: for that which was wanting to me, the brothers supplied who came from Macedonia. And in all things I have kept myself from being burthensome to you: and so I will keep myself.
changes.reason: Egerem means “I was in need” and nulli onerosus fui “I was a burden to no one”; “wanted” and “chargeable” mislead a modern listener.

changes.before: In labor and painfulness, in much watchings, in hunger and thirst, in fastings often, in cold and nakedness:
changes.after: In labor and painfulness, in many watchings, in hunger and thirst, in fastings often, in cold and nakedness:
changes.reason: Vigiliis multis is plural (“many watchings”); “much watchings” is ungrammatical aloud.

changes.before: Besides those things which are without: my daily instance, the anxiety for all the churches.
changes.after: Besides those things which are without: the daily pressure upon me, the anxiety for all the churches.
changes.reason: Instantia mea quotidiana is the pressure that presses on Paul daily; “instance” no longer carries that sense.

changes.before: I know a man in Christ who was caught up to the third heaven fourteen years ago. Whether in the body or out of the body, I do not know. God knows.
changes.after: I know a man in Christ who was caught up to the third heaven fourteen years ago. Whether in the body, I do not know, or out of the body, I do not know. God knows.
changes.reason: The Latin repeats nescio after each alternative (sive in corpore nescio, sive extra corpus nescio), a deliberate repetition the column dropped.

changes.before: For which cause I please myself in my infirmities, in reproaches, in necessities, in persecutions, in distresses, for Christ. For when I am weak, then am I powerful.
changes.after: For which cause I take pleasure in my infirmities, in reproaches, in necessities, in persecutions, in distresses, for Christ. For when I am weak, then am I powerful.
changes.reason: Placeo mihi means “I am well pleased, take pleasure”; “I please myself” sounds like self-indulgence aloud.

changes.before: I desired Titus: and I sent with him a brother. Did Titus overreach you? Did we not walk with the same spirit? Did we not in the same steps?
changes.after: I asked Titus: and I sent with him a brother. Did Titus overreach you? Did we not walk with the same spirit? Did we not walk in the same steps?
changes.reason: Rogavi Titum means “I asked Titus,” and the elliptical “Did we not in the same steps?” needs its verb (ambulavimus) to be followed aloud.

changes.before: to reveal his Son in me so that I might proclaim him among the Gentiles, I did not immediately yield to flesh and blood,
changes.after: to reveal his Son in me so that I might proclaim him among the Gentiles, immediately I did not yield to flesh and blood,
changes.reason: Continuo non acquievi means that at once Paul did not consult flesh and blood; “did not immediately yield” implies he yielded later.

changes.before: I have confidence in you in the Lord that you will be of no other mind. But whoever troubles you will bear the judgment.
changes.after: I have confidence in you in the Lord that you will be of no other mind. But he who troubles you will bear the judgment, whoever he may be.
changes.reason: The clause quicumque est ille (“whoever he may be”) was omitted.

changes.before: Let us not grow weary in doing good, for in due season we will reap if we do not give up.
changes.after: Let us not grow weary in doing good, for in due season we will reap if we do not grow weary.
changes.reason: The Latin repeats the same verb (non deficiamus … non deficientes), and the column’s first “grow weary” should be echoed.

changes.before: Look at the letters I have written to you with my own hand.
changes.after: See what kind of letters I have written to you in my own hand.
changes.reason: Qualibus litteris means “with what letters,” drawing attention to the handwriting itself, which the flat “the letters” loses.

changes.before: Cease not to give thanks for you, making commemoration of you in my prayers,
changes.after: Do not cease to give thanks for you, making commemoration of you in my prayers,
changes.reason: The subject is the “I” of 1:15 (non cesso); “Cease not” at the head of the verse sounds like a command to the listener.

changes.before: In which also we all conversed in time past, in the desires of our flesh, fulfilling the will of the flesh and of our thoughts, and were by nature children of wrath, even as the rest:
changes.after: In which also we all lived in time past, in the desires of our flesh, fulfilling the will of the flesh and of our thoughts, and were by nature children of wrath, even as the rest:
changes.reason: Conversati sumus means “we lived, conducted ourselves”; modern “conversed” is heard as “talked.”

changes.before: And has raised us up together and has made us sit together in the heavenly places, through Christ Jesus.
changes.after: And has raised us up together and has made us sit together in the heavenly places, in Christ Jesus.
changes.reason: The Latin has in Christo Jesu, the same “in Christ” formula the column keeps in 2:7 and 2:10.

changes.before: But now in Christ Jesus, you, who some time were afar off, are made near by the blood of Christ.
changes.after: But now in Christ Jesus, you, who once were afar off, are made near by the blood of Christ.
changes.reason: Aliquando means “once, formerly”; “some time” is heard as “for a while.”

changes.before: Now therefore you are no more strangers and foreigners: but you are fellow citizens with the saints and the domestics of God,
changes.after: Now therefore you are no more strangers and foreigners: but you are fellow citizens with the saints and members of the household of God,
changes.reason: Domestici Dei are members of God’s household; “domestics” is heard as household servants.

changes.before: As you reading, may understand my knowledge in the mystery of Christ,
changes.after: As, by reading, you can understand my knowledge in the mystery of Christ,
changes.reason: Prout potestis legentes intelligere means “as you are able, by reading, to understand”; “As you reading, may understand” trips the ear and weakens potestis to a wish.

changes.before: And he gave some apostles, and some prophets, and other some evangelists, and other some pastors and doctors:
changes.after: And he gave some as apostles, and some as prophets, and others as evangelists, and others as pastors and doctors:
changes.reason: The archaic “other some” for alios is hard to follow aloud; “some as … others as” keeps the Latin’s quosdam/alios pattern.

changes.before: To put off, according to former conversation, the old man, who is corrupted according to the desire of error.
changes.after: To put off, according to your former way of life, the old man, who is corrupted according to the desires of error.
changes.reason: Pristinam conversationem means former way of life (“conversation” now misleads a listener), and desideria erroris is plural.

changes.before: And do not be drunk with wine, wherein is luxury: but be filled with the Holy Spirit,
changes.after: And do not be drunk with wine, wherein is debauchery: but be filled with the Holy Spirit,
changes.reason: Luxuria here is debauchery or dissipation; modern “luxury” suggests comfort and wealth, which the Latin does not say.

changes.before: By all prayer and supplication praying at all times in the spirit: and in the same watching with all instance and supplication for all the saints:
changes.after: By all prayer and supplication praying at all times in the spirit: and in the same watching with all perseverance and supplication for all the saints:
changes.reason: In omni instantia means with all perseverance; the archaic “instance” is meaningless to a modern listener.

changes.before: For your communication in the gospel of Christ, from the first day until now.
changes.after: For your fellowship in the gospel of Christ, from the first day until now.
changes.reason: Communicatio here is fellowship or sharing; “communication” now suggests talking, which the Latin does not mean.

changes.before: As it is meet for me to think this for you all, for that I have you in my heart; and that, in my bands and in the defence and confirmation of the gospel, you all are partakers of my joy.
changes.after: As it is right for me to think this for you all, for that I have you in my heart; and that, in my chains and in the defence and confirmation of the gospel, you all are partakers of my joy.
changes.reason: Archaic “meet” (justum) and “bands” (vinculis) trip a listener; “right” and “chains” say the same thing, matching “in chains” in Colossians 4:3.

changes.before: So that my bands are made manifest in Christ, in all the court and in all other places.
changes.after: So that my chains are made manifest in Christ, in all the court and in all other places.
changes.reason: Vincula mea are Paul’s chains; “bands” is easily misheard aloud and the column already says “in chains” in Colossians 4:3.

changes.before: And many of the brothers in the Lord, growing confident by my bands, are much more bold to speak the word of God without fear.
changes.after: And many of the brothers in the Lord, growing confident by my chains, are much more bold to speak the word of God without fear.
changes.reason: Vinculis meis means by my chains; archaic “bands” is easily misheard aloud.

changes.before: And some out of contention preach Christ not sincerely: supposing that they raise affliction to my bands.
changes.after: And some out of contention preach Christ not sincerely: supposing that they stir up affliction for my chains.
changes.reason: Pressuram se suscitare vinculis meis means they think to stir up affliction for (add it to) my chains; “raise affliction to my bands” is obscure aloud.

changes.before: Only let your conversation be worthy of the gospel of Christ: that, whether I come and see you, or, being absent, may hear of you, that you stand fast in one spirit, with one mind laboring together for the faith of the gospel.
changes.after: Only let your manner of life be worthy of the gospel of Christ: that, whether I come and see you, or, being absent, may hear of you, that you stand fast in one spirit, with one mind laboring together for the faith of the gospel.
changes.reason: Conversamini means conduct yourselves or live; “conversation” now suggests speech, which narrows and misstates the Latin.

changes.before: If there be therefore any consolation in Christ, if any comfort of love, if any society of the spirit, if any heart of commiseration:
changes.after: If there be therefore any consolation in Christ, if any comfort of love, if any fellowship of the spirit, if any heart of commiseration:
changes.reason: Societas spiritus is fellowship in the spirit (the column renders societatem as “fellowship” in 3:10); “society” misleads aloud.

changes.before: According to zeal, persecuting the church of God: According to the justice that is in the law, conversing without blame.
changes.after: According to zeal, persecuting the church of God: According to the justice that is in the law, living without blame.
changes.reason: Conversatus sine querela means having lived blamelessly; “conversing” now means talking, which the Latin does not say.

changes.before: Nevertheless, you have done well in communicating to my tribulation.
changes.after: Nevertheless, you have done well in sharing in my tribulation.
changes.reason: Communicantes tribulationi meae means sharing in my tribulation; “communicating to” now suggests sending a message.

changes.before: And you also know, O Philippians, that in the beginning of the gospel, when I departed from Macedonia, no church communicated with me as concerning giving and receiving, but you only.
changes.after: And you also know, O Philippians, that in the beginning of the gospel, when I departed from Macedonia, no church shared with me in the matter of giving and receiving, but you only.
changes.reason: Communicavit in ratione dati et accepti means shared with me in an account of giving and receiving; “communicated with me as concerning” is obscure and misleading aloud.

changes.before: Greet you every saint in Christ Jesus.
changes.after: Greet every saint in Christ Jesus.
changes.reason: Salutate is an imperative; “Greet you every saint” can be heard as Paul greeting each saint himself.

changes.before: And you, whereas you were some time alienated and enemies in mind in evil works:
changes.after: And you, whereas you were once alienated and enemies in mind in evil works:
changes.reason: Aliquando means once or formerly; archaic “some time” is heard as “for a while”.

changes.before: In which you also walked some time, when you lived in them.
changes.after: In which you also once walked, when you lived in them.
changes.reason: Ambulastis aliquando means you once walked; archaic “some time” is heard as “for a while”.

changes.before: All whatever you do in word or in work, do all in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, giving thanks to God and the Father by him.
changes.after: Whatever you do in word or in work, do all in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, giving thanks to God and the Father by him.
changes.reason: Omne quodcumque is simply “whatever”; “All whatever” trips the ear, and the following “do all” keeps the Latin’s omnia.

changes.before: Be instant in prayer: watching in it with thanksgiving.
changes.after: Be persistent in prayer: watching in it with thanksgiving.
changes.reason: Orationi instate means persist in prayer; archaic “instant” now means immediate and misleads a listener.

changes.before: Aristarchus, my fellow prisoner, greets you: and Mark, the cousin german of Barnabas, touching whom you have received commandments. If he come to you, receive him.
changes.after: Aristarchus, my fellow prisoner, greets you: and Mark, the cousin of Barnabas, concerning whom you have received commandments. If he come to you, receive him.
changes.reason: Consobrinus is simply a cousin, and the archaic “cousin german … touching whom” is hard to follow aloud.

changes.before: And say to Archippus: Take care to the ministry which you have received in the Lord, that you fulfill it.
changes.after: And say to Archippus: See to the ministry which you have received in the Lord, that you fulfill it.
changes.reason: Vide ministerium means see to or look after the ministry; “Take care to the ministry” is ungrammatical aloud.

changes.before: The greeting of Paul with my own hand. Be mindful of my bands. Grace be with you. Amen.
changes.after: The greeting of Paul with my own hand. Be mindful of my chains. Grace be with you. Amen.
changes.reason: Vinculorum meorum are Paul’s chains; archaic “bands” is easily misheard, and 4:3 already says “in chains”.

changes.before: For which cause, I also suffer these things: but I am not ashamed. For I know whom I have believed and I am certain that he is able to keep that which I have committed to him, against that day.
changes.after: For which cause, I also suffer these things: but I am not ashamed. For I know whom I have believed and I am certain that he is able to keep that which I have committed to him, until that day.
changes.reason: Archaic “against that day” is heard as opposition; in illum diem means until that day.

changes.before: Keep the good thing committed to your trust by the Holy Spirit who dwells in us.
changes.after: Keep the good thing committed to your trust, through the Holy Spirit who dwells in us.
changes.reason: Aloud it sounded as if the Spirit committed the deposit; per Spiritum Sanctum goes with custodi (keep it through the Spirit).

changes.before: No man, being a soldier to God, entangles himself with secular businesses: that he may please him to whom he has engaged himself.
changes.after: No man, being a soldier to God, entangles himself with secular affairs: that he may please him to whom he has engaged himself.
changes.reason: “Businesses” now suggests commercial firms; negotiis saecularibus are worldly affairs.

changes.before: For he also that strives for the mastery is not crowned, except he strive lawfully.
changes.after: For he also who competes in the games is not crowned unless he has competed lawfully.
changes.reason: Archaic “strives for the mastery … except he strive” trips the ear; certat in agone is competing in the games.

changes.before: The husbandman that labors must first partake of the fruits.
changes.after: The farmer that labors must first partake of the fruits.
changes.reason: “Husbandman” is easily misheard as husband; agricola is a farmer.

changes.before: Wherein I labor even to bands, as an evildoer. But the word of God is not bound.
changes.after: Wherein I labor even to chains, as an evildoer. But the word of God is not bound.
changes.reason: Archaic “bands” is unclear aloud; vincula are chains.

changes.before: And their speech spreads like a canker: of whom are Hymeneus and Philetus:
changes.after: And their speech spreads like a cancer: of whom are Hymeneus and Philetus:
changes.reason: “Canker” is obscure to listeners; the Latin image is cancer, a spreading sore.

changes.before: Preach the word: be instant in season, out of season: reprove, entreat, rebuke in all patience and doctrine.
changes.after: Preach the word: be urgent in season, out of season: reprove, entreat, rebuke in all patience and doctrine.
changes.reason: Archaic “be instant” no longer means press on; insta = be urgent, persist.

changes.before: Whom do you also avoid: for he has greatly withstood our words.
changes.after: Avoid him yourself also: for he has greatly withstood our words.
changes.reason: “Whom do you also avoid” sounds like a question; quem et tu devita is a command.

changes.before: At my first answer, no one stood with me: but all forsook me. May it not be laid to their charge!
changes.after: At my first defense, no one stood with me: but all forsook me. May it not be laid to their charge!
changes.reason: Archaic legal “answer” is unclear; defensio is his defense before the court.

changes.before: For it became him for whom are all things and by whom are all things, who had brought many children into glory, to perfect the author of their salvation, by his passion.
changes.after: For it was fitting for him, for whom are all things and by whom are all things, who had brought many children into glory, to perfect the author of their salvation, by his passion.
changes.reason: Archaic “it became him” is heard as turned into; decebat = it was fitting.

changes.before: Therefore, it behoved him in all things to be made like to his brothers, that he might become a merciful and faithful high priest before God, that he might be a propitiation for the sins of the people.
changes.after: Therefore he ought in all things to be made like to his brothers, that he might become a merciful and faithful high priest before God, that he might be a propitiation for the sins of the people.
changes.reason: Archaic “it behoved him” trips the ear; debuit = he ought.

changes.before: There remains therefore a day of rest for the people of God.
changes.after: There remains therefore a sabbath rest for the people of God.
changes.reason: Sabbatismus keeps the image of the sabbath, which the argument from God’s seventh-day rest depends on.

changes.before: For every high priest taken from among men is ordained for men in the things that appertain to God, that he may offer up gifts and sacrifices for sins:
changes.after: For every high priest taken from among men is ordained for men in the things that pertain to God, that he may offer up gifts and sacrifices for sins:
changes.reason: Archaic “appertain” modernised for the ear; meaning unchanged (quae sunt ad Deum).

changes.before: And being consummated, he became, to all that obey him, the cause of eternal salvation:
changes.after: And being made perfect, he became, to all that obey him, the cause of eternal salvation:
changes.reason: “Consummated” now carries the wrong sense aloud; consummatus here means made perfect.

changes.before: For the earth, that drinks in the rain which comes often upon it and brings forth herbs meet for them by whom it is tilled, receives blessing from God.
changes.after: For the earth, that drinks in the rain which comes often upon it and brings forth herbs fit for them by whom it is tilled, receives blessing from God.
changes.reason: Archaic “meet” (heard as meat/meet) modernised; opportunam = fit, suitable.

changes.before: For the priesthood being translated, it is necessary that a translation also be made of the law,
changes.after: For the priesthood being changed, it is necessary that a change also be made of the law,
changes.reason: “Translated” now means rendering into another language; translatio here is a change or transfer.

changes.before: And the others indeed were made many priests, because by reason of death they were not suffered to continue:
changes.after: And the others indeed were made many priests, because by reason of death they were not permitted to continue:
changes.reason: Archaic “suffered” (allowed) is heard as endured; prohiberentur = were prevented.

changes.before: For the law makes men priests, who have infirmity: but the word of the oath (which was since the law) the Son who is perfected forever.
changes.after: For the law makes men priests, who have infirmity: but the word of the oath (which came after the law) makes the Son, who is perfected forever.
changes.reason: Supplies the verb carried over from constituit and clarifies post legem, which “was since the law” obscured aloud.

changes.before: And on the one hand indeed, by reproaches and tribulations, were made a gazingstock; and on the other, became companions of them that were used in such sort.
changes.after: And on the one hand indeed, by reproaches and tribulations, were made a spectacle; and on the other, became companions of them that were so treated.
changes.reason: Archaic “gazingstock” and “used in such sort” trip the ear; spectaculum, taliter conversantium.

changes.before: For you both had compassion on them that were in bands and took with joy the being stripped of your own goods, knowing that you have a better and a lasting substance.
changes.after: For you both had compassion on them that were in chains and took with joy the plundering of your own goods, knowing that you have a better and a lasting substance.
changes.reason: Archaic “bands” and the awkward “the being stripped of” smoothed; vinctis, rapinam bonorum.

changes.before: And others had trial of mockeries and stripes: moreover also of bands and prisons.
changes.after: And others had trial of mockeries and stripes: moreover also of chains and prisons.
changes.reason: Archaic “bands” is unclear aloud; vincula are chains.

changes.before: Lest there be any sexually immoral person or profane person, as Esau who for one mess sold his first birthright.
changes.after: Lest there be any sexually immoral person or profane person, as Esau who for one meal sold his birthright.
changes.reason: Primitiva sua is simply his birthright (his rights as firstborn), and the Douay “for one mess … his first birthright” trips a listener with an archaic word for a meal and a doubled sense of “first.”

changes.before: And I implore you, brothers, that you suffer this word of consolation. For I have written to you in a few words.
changes.after: And I implore you, brothers, that you bear with this word of consolation. For I have written to you in a few words.
changes.reason: Ut sufferatis verbum solatii asks them to bear with or put up with the letter; heard aloud, “that you suffer this word” sounds as if the word will cause them suffering.

changes.before: My brothers, have not the faith of our Lord Jesus Christ of glory, with respect of persons.
changes.after: My brothers, do not hold the faith of our Lord Jesus Christ of glory with respect of persons.
changes.reason: Nolite … habere fidem is a prohibition (“do not hold the faith … with respect of persons”); the archaic “have not the faith” sounds aloud like a statement that they lack the faith.

changes.before: And you have respect to him that is clothed with the fine apparel and shall say to him: Sit you here well: but say to the poor man: Stand you there, or: Sit under my footstool:
changes.after: And you have respect to him that is clothed with the fine apparel and shall say to him: You, sit here in a good place: but say to the poor man: You, stand there, or: Sit under my footstool:
changes.reason: Tu sede hic bene means “you, sit here in a good place” (a seat of honour), set against tu sta illic; the Douay “Sit you here well” is unclear when heard.

changes.before: So speak you and so do, as being to be judged by the law of liberty.
changes.after: So speak and so act, as those who are to be judged by the law of liberty.
changes.reason: Sicut per legem libertatis incipientes judicari means “as those who are to be judged by the law of liberty”; “as being to be judged” is hard to follow aloud.

changes.before: So also the tongue is a small member, yet it boasts of great things. See what a fire can set so great a forest ablaze!
changes.after: So also the tongue is a small member, yet it boasts of great things. See how small a fire sets so great a forest ablaze!
